languages.name: Python

topics.title: Setup, running code & first program
topics.definition: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language. You write human-readable code in a .py file and the Python interpreter runs it line by line, without a separate compile step.
topics.analogy: Like a cooking show host who reads your recipe aloud and cooks each step immediately: write a line, Python does it at once. Installing Python is like setting up your kitchen before cooking.
keyPoints: Install Python 3.10+ and check it with `python --version`; on some systems the command is `python3`.
A .py file is plain text: write code in any editor, run it with `python file.py` from that folder.
`print()` shows output on screen; `input()` pauses and reads what the user types (always as text).
Indentation (4 spaces) defines blocks: everything lined up under `if` or `for` belongs to it — inconsistent spaces cause IndentationError.
Create one virtual environment per project (`python -m venv .venv`) so libraries never clash between projects.
Guard runnable code with `if __name__ == "__main__":` so the file can also be safely imported as a module.

advancedExamples.title: Command-line greeter with argparse
advancedExamples.code:
import argparse

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Greeter")
    parser.add_argument("city", help="city to greet")
    parser.add_argument("--loud", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    msg = f"Learning from {args.city}"
    print(msg.upper() if args.loud else msg)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
advancedExamples.note: Turns a script into a real CLI with validation and free --help output.

interview.question: Interpreted vs compiled: how does Python run code?
interview.answer: Python compiles source to bytecode (.pyc) automatically, then the interpreter (CPython VM) executes it — you never invoke a compiler manually, but syntax errors still stop the program before running.

interview.question: What does `if __name__ == "__main__":` do?
interview.answer: When run directly, the file’s __name__ is "__main__"; when imported it is the module name. The guard lets one file be both a script and a reusable module.

interview.question: How do you isolate project dependencies?
interview.answer: python -m venv .venv creates a private environment; activate it, then pip install so each project keeps its own library versions.

interview.question: Why does input() math surprise beginners?
interview.answer: input() always returns a string, so "5" + "5" is "55". Convert first: int(input(...)) for numbers, and handle ValueError for bad input.

intro: Python is a high-level, interpreted language. You write human-readable code in a .py file, and the interpreter runs it line by line — no separate compile step. This lesson gets you from a blank file to a working first program.

You install Python 3.10+, open a terminal, and run python file.py from the folder that holds your script. The print() function shows output; input() pauses and reads what the user types (always as text).
The first line you will type is a greeting: print("Namaste, CodeAtlas!"). Saving and running it correctly is a small victory — every other lesson starts from this exact step.

Common traps: using smart quotes in source code, saving with a wrong extension, and — the most famous — inconsistent indentation. Python uses 4 spaces per level; mixing tabs and spaces raises an IndentationError.
Once you can run code and read errors, the rest of Python is the same loop: write, run, read the message, fix, repeat.

topics.title: Variables, data types & operators
topics.definition: Variables are named boxes that store values. Python has built-in data types — int, float, str, bool, None — and operators (+, -, *, /, %, ==, and, or, not) to compute and compare them.
topics.analogy: Like labelled dabbas in an Indian kitchen: sugar dabba holds sugar (string), rice dabba holds a quantity (number). Operators are the cooking actions — mix (add), compare (taste-test), combine (and/or).
keyPoints: Use snake_case names (student_marks); names can hold any type and can be reassigned.
int (5), float (5.5), str ("Asha"), bool (True/False), NoneType (None) are the core types; check with type(x).
Arithmetic: + - * / (float division), // (floor), % (remainder), ** (power).
Comparison (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) returns True/False; combine with and, or, not.
Convert explicitly: int("5") -> 5, str(5) -> "5"; int("five") raises ValueError.
None means "no value yet" — check with `is None`, never `== None` in clean code.

interview.question: Dynamic typing: what is it and what can go wrong?
interview.answer: Variables have no fixed type, so the same name can hold an int then a string. Flexible, but a surprise type causes TypeError at runtime — hence type hints and tests.

interview.question: == vs is — when does it matter?
interview.answer: == compares values ("a" == "a" is True); is compares identity (same object). Use is only for None/singletons, never for numbers or strings.

interview.question: What is None and how do you test for it?
interview.answer: None is the absence of a value. Test with `x is None` because `==` can be overloaded and behave unexpectedly.

interview.question: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in Python?
interview.answer: Floats are binary approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with round() or math.isclose(), or use Decimal for money.

topics.title: Strings & text handling
topics.definition: Strings (str) hold text. They support indexing, slicing, methods (upper, strip, split, join), concatenation with +, and interpolation with f-strings: f"Hello {name}".
topics.analogy: Like a garland of marigold flowers: each flower is a character at a position; slicing takes a section of the garland; split separates it into individual flowers; join re-threads them with new string.
keyPoints: Create with single, double or triple quotes; triple quotes span multiple lines.
Index from 0 (s[0] is first); negative index s[-1] is the last character; slice s[0:5] takes a range.
f-strings embed expressions: f"{price * 1.18:.2f}" formats GST-inclusive price to 2 decimals.
Key methods: upper/lower, strip (trim spaces), split (text->list), join (list->text), replace, startswith.
Strings are immutable: methods return new strings; s.upper() never changes s itself.
Convert carefully: int("42") works, int("4.2") fails (use float first); str(42) goes the other way.

interview.question: Why are Python strings immutable, and what follows from it?
interview.answer: Characters cannot change in place, so every method returns a new string. Enables safe sharing, hashing (dict keys), and thread safety; repeated += in loops is O(n^2) — build lists and join instead.

interview.question: f-string vs .format() vs % — which and when?
interview.answer: f-strings for nearly everything (fastest, most readable); .format() for templates stored separately; % is legacy. f-strings support full expressions and format specs like {x:.2f}.

interview.question: Explain slicing s[a:b:c] precisely.
interview.answer: From index a (inclusive) to b (exclusive), stepping by c. Defaults 0/len/1; negatives count from the end; s[::-1] reverses. Out-of-range slices clip silently instead of erroring.

interview.question: strip() vs lstrip() vs rstrip()?
interview.answer: strip removes leading+trailing whitespace (or given chars); lstrip left only; rstrip right only. None touches the middle — use replace for that.

You install Python 3.10+, open a terminal, and run python file.py from the folder that holds your script. The print() function shows output; input() pauses and reads what the user types (always as text).
The first line you will type is a greeting: print("Namaste, CodeAtlas!"). Saving and running it correctly is a small victory — every other lesson starts from this exact step.

topics.title: Conditions: if, elif, else & match
topics.definition: Conditions let programs choose: if runs a block when its test is True, elif tries the next test, else catches the rest. match (Python 3.10+) picks a branch by pattern, and the ternary fits a two-way choice in one line.
topics.analogy: Like a traffic policeman at a busy signal: if an ambulance comes, clear the lane; elif a VIP convoy comes, hold traffic; else let everyone flow. match is the toll plaza — each vehicle type has its own exact lane.
keyPoints: Only one branch runs: the first test that is True; else needs no test and catches everything left.
Compare with ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=; combine with and, or, not; chain ranges like 18 <= age <= 60.
Empty values are falsy ("", 0, [], None) — write `if name:` to mean "if name is non-empty".
Ternary packs a choice: status = "pass" if marks >= 40 else "fail".
match checks one value against patterns: case "Mon": ... with case _ as the default.
Never write `== True`; write `if passed:` — and indent every branch with 4 spaces.

interview.question: What values are falsy in Python?
interview.answer: None, False, 0, 0.0, "", [], (), {}, set() - everything else is truthy. That is why `if items:` safely means "non-empty".

interview.question: if/elif/else vs match - when is match better?
interview.answer: match shines when branching one value against many exact patterns (commands, statuses) with destructuring; if/elif wins for ranges and complex boolean logic.

interview.question: Explain short-circuiting in `a and b` / `a or b`.
interview.answer: and stops at the first falsy value (returns it); or stops at the first truthy one. Used for guards and defaults - but beware falsy-but-valid 0 and "".

interview.question: Why avoid deep nesting? Show the fix.
interview.answer: Each level doubles mental paths. Invert conditions into guard clauses with early return/raise so the main logic stays flat and readable.

topics.title: Loops: for, while & comprehensions
topics.definition: Loops repeat work: for walks items directly, while repeats while a test holds, comprehensions build lists in one line. break exits, continue skips, else on a loop runs when no break happened.
topics.analogy: Like a temple prasadam line: for serves each person in queue one by one; while keeps serving until the vessel empties; a comprehension is the pre-packed laddu box line - same sweet for everyone, packed in one motion.
keyPoints: for x in items walks values directly - prefer it over index juggling whenever possible.
range(n) gives 0..n-1; range(1, 6) gives 1..5; range(0, 10, 2) steps by 2.
while needs progress toward its exit (counter/found flag) or it loops forever.
break exits the loop; continue skips to the next round; loop-else runs only without break.
List comprehensions: [x*x for x in nums if x > 0] filters and maps in one readable line.
Iterate dicts with .items() for key+value; use enumerate() when you also need the index.

interview.question: for vs while - which when?
interview.answer: for: known/iterable-driven rounds (lists, ranges). while: unknown rounds ending on a condition (retry until success, read until EOF). Mismatching them causes index bugs or infinite loops.

interview.question: How does loop-else work?
interview.answer: else after for/while runs only if the loop finished WITHOUT break. Perfect for search-found vs search-missed logic without extra flags.

interview.question: Comprehension vs map/filter?
interview.answer: Comprehensions are more readable for simple transforms and faster to write; map/filter win when reusing an existing named function. Avoid nested comprehensions past 2 levels.

interview.question: break vs continue vs pass?
interview.answer: break exits the loop; continue jumps to the next round; pass does nothing (a placeholder keeping syntax valid). Mixing break/continue up inverts the logic.

topics.title: Functions: def, arguments & return
topics.definition: Functions package steps into reusable blocks: def names them, parameters receive input, return sends a result back. Default args, *args and **kwargs make functions flexible.
topics.analogy: Like a tiffin caterer with a standard order form: you fill items (arguments), the kitchen cooks (body), and returns packed boxes (return value). Default items are the fixed menu; *args is the extra-addons list.
keyPoints: def add(a, b): defines; add(4, 6) calls; return sends the result back and exits.
Positional args match by order; keyword args (add(b=6, a=4)) match by name.
Defaults fill gaps: def fee(age=10) uses 10 when omitted - defaults must come last.
*args collects extra positionals into a tuple; **kwargs collects named extras into a dict.
Variables assigned inside are local; use return to get values out - avoid globals.
Docstrings ("""...""") document the function; type hints (def f(x: int) -> int) aid readers.

topics.title: Collections: list, tuple, set & dict

topics.title: Errors, files & modules

topics.title: OOP: classes & objects
topics.definition: A class is a blueprint that bundles data (attributes) with the functions working on that data (methods). An object is one concrete thing built from the blueprint, holding its own values.
topics.analogy: Like a railway ticket form: the blank form (class) defines the fields; each filled ticket (object) has its own name and seat. Methods are the actions a ticket supports - confirm, cancel, upgrade.

self is the object itself: every method takes self first and reads or writes self.marks.
Create instances with s = Student("Asha", 92) - Python calls __init__ automatically.
Methods add behaviour: def passed(self): return self.marks >= 40.
__str__ controls print(s); without it you see a raw object address.
Class attributes are shared by all objects; self.x attributes belong to one object only.

interview.question: Class vs object vs instance?
interview.answer: Class is the blueprint; object/instance is one built thing with its own data. Many instances share the class methods but hold different attribute values.

interview.question: What is self really?
interview.answer: The instance the method was called on, passed automatically as the first argument. Forgetting it misaligns all parameters.

interview.question: __init__ vs __str__ vs __repr__?

interview.question: Class attribute vs instance attribute bug?

topics.title: Collection methods & comprehensions
topics.definition: Beyond basics: list methods (append, extend, sort), dict get/update/items, set ops, plus comprehensions [x for x in data if ok] that build collections in one readable line.
topics.analogy: Like packing a tiffin efficiently: append adds one roti, extend empties a whole plate in, dict.get asks "is sabzi there?" without dropping the box, and a comprehension is packing all non-spicy items in one pass.

dict.get(k, default) avoids KeyError; update() merges; items() loops key+value together.
Comprehension: [m+5 for m in marks if m < 90] filters and transforms in one line.
Set ops (| union, & intersect, - difference) answer "common / only-here" questions fast.
sort() sorts in place; sorted(data) returns a new sorted copy; key=len sorts by length.

interview.answer: Membership tests, dedup, and common/only comparisons - O(1) average lookup vs O(n) list scan, plus union/intersect/difference operators.

topics.title: Iterators, generators & async basics
topics.definition: Iterators produce values one at a time with next(); generators (yield) create lazy sequences; async/await (asyncio) runs I/O tasks concurrently without threads.
topics.analogy: Like a dosa counter: an iterator serves one dosa per token (next()); a generator is the cook making each dosa only when ordered (lazy, no pile-up); async is one waiter taking many tables orders while the kitchen works - nobody blocks.
keyPoints: iter() + next() walk manually; StopIteration ends the stream - for loops hide this.
Generator: def gen(): yield x pauses and resumes - memory-flat for lakh-item streams.
Generator expressions (x*x for x in data) are lazy; list(...) forces the whole result.
async def + await pauses on I/O; asyncio.run(main()) drives the event loop.
gather() runs many awaits together; total time is the slowest, not the sum.
Generators are single-pass: once consumed they are empty - re-create to re-read.

basicExamples.code:

it = iter(nums)
print(next(it))

lineByLine.explanation: Second call: 20; a third would raise StopIteration.

guidedExamples.title: gather concurrency
guidedExamples.code:
import asyncio

async def serve(item):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return item

async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(serve("idli"), serve("dosa")))

asyncio.run(main())

advancedExamples.note: Chained generators filter/transform streams stage by stage - each item flows through without storing the whole list.

advancedExamples.title: Async with timeout guard
advancedExamples.code:
import asyncio

async def slow():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    return "late"

async def main():
    try:
        print(await asyncio.wait_for(slow(), timeout=0.2))
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        print("too slow, moved on")

asyncio.run(main())
advancedExamples.note: wait_for caps a coroutine: slow I/O becomes a caught TimeoutError instead of a hung program.

interview.question: Iterator vs iterable?
interview.answer: Iterable has __iter__ (makes iterators: lists, files). Iterator has __next__ and state (it itself). for calls iter() then next() until StopIteration.

interview.question: How does yield save memory?
interview.answer: The generator pauses per item - only one value exists at a time. A list of 10 lakh rows eats RAM; a generator streams them flat.

interview.question: async/await vs threads?
interview.answer: Async: one thread, cooperative pauses at await - cheap for I/O-bound (10k connections). Threads: OS-managed, better for CPU work but heavier; GIL limits Python thread parallelism.

interview.question: Why is a generator exhausted after one pass?
interview.answer: It holds a position pointer, not the data. Consuming advances to the end; there is no rewind - call the factory again for a fresh stream.

intro: This topic, "Iterators, generators & async basics", is your step into a bigger idea, and it builds directly on everything you have learned so far. We will start from the very beginning: what this concept actually means, why it exists, and how it is used in everyday programs — never assuming you already know the jargon.

At its core, iterators produce values one at a time with next(); generators (yield) create lazy sequences; async/await (asyncio) runs i/o tasks concurrently without threads.. If you are not sure of a word we use, pause and check it: each one is defined in plain language in the key points that follow.

Think about it through a real-world analogy before touching code: Like a dosa counter: an iterator serves one dosa per token (next()); a generator is the cook making each dosa only when ordered (lazy, no pile-up); async is one waiter taking many tables orders while the kitchen works - nobody blocks.. This mental picture is the fastest way to remember the shape of the idea when you meet it again in a real project.

The key points below are the minimum you need. Notice how each one connects to the last — that is how knowledge sticks. After each point you will see a tiny example you can run, followed by one that slowly grows in difficulty, so you can watch the idea work from start to finish.
Never stop at reading the examples. Type them into your editor, change a value, break it on purpose, and read the error. That loop — write, run, break, fix — is where the concept becomes yours.

Finally, test yourself with the practice questions and the interview questions. The interview questions are the "why" behind the "how": they are the ones that reappear in real work and in technical interviews, and we have written them to be answerable from the explanations above.

topics.title: Testing, debugging & virtual environments
topics.definition: Virtual environments (venv) isolate each projects packages; pip installs libraries; pytest or assert checks prove code works; tracebacks and print/debugger inspection fix what fails.
topics.analogy: Like a tiffin trial kitchen: venv is a separate counter so masala tests never spoil the main order; pip fetches ingredients; taste-tests (asserts) catch salt errors before delivery; the traceback is the complaint slip pointing at the exact counter.
keyPoints: python -m venv .venv then source .venv/bin/activate (or .venv Scripts activate on Windows) isolates packages.
pip install requests installs into the active env; pip freeze > requirements.txt records exact versions.
assert add(2, 3) == 5 stops loudly on failure - the simplest possible test.
pytest runs test_*.py files; one failing test names the exact function and values.
Read tracebacks bottom-up: last line is the error, above lines are the call path.
Catch specific errors (ValueError) never bare except; log or re-raise what you cannot handle.

intro: Python is a high-level, interpreted language. You write human-readable code in a .py file, and the interpreter runs it line by line — no separate compile step. This lesson gets you from a blank file to a working first program.

You install Python 3.10+, open a terminal, and run python file.py from the folder that holds your script. The print() function shows output; input() pauses and reads what the user types (always as text).
The first line you will type is a greeting: print("Namaste, CodeAtlas!"). Saving and running it correctly is a small victory — every other lesson starts from this exact step.

Common traps: using smart quotes in source code, saving with a wrong extension, and — the most famous — inconsistent indentation. Python uses 4 spaces per level; mixing tabs and spaces raises an IndentationError.
Once you can run code and read errors, the rest of Python is the same loop: write, run, read the message, fix, repeat.

topics.title: Setup, running code & first program
topics.definition: JavaScript (JS) is a high-level, interpreted language that runs in browsers and on servers via Node.js. You write code in .js files or <script> tags and a JS engine (V8, SpiderMonkey) executes it.
topics.analogy: Like a street magician who performs instantly wherever there is a crowd: the same JS trick runs in the browser, on a server, even in a mobile app — no stage setup, just perform.
keyPoints: Run browser JS: open DevTools (F12) Console and type code; run files with Node.js via `node file.js`.
`console.log()` prints output; `prompt()` (browser) reads text input, always as a string.
Statements end with newlines (semicolons optional but recommended in teams); { } braces define blocks.
`let` (changeable), `const` (one-time binding), `var` (old, function-scoped — avoid in new code).
JS is dynamically typed: a variable can hold a number, then a string; check with typeof x.
One language, many runtimes: browser APIs (DOM, fetch) exist only in browsers; fs/process only in Node.

interview.question: How does JavaScript run in browser vs Node?

interview.question: let vs const vs var?

interview.question: What does "use strict" change?

topics.title: Types, operators & equality
topics.definition: JS has primitive types (number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint) and objects (including arrays and functions). Operators (+, -, *, /, %, ===, &&, ||, !) compute and compare; === checks value AND type with no conversion.
topics.analogy: Like currency notes vs coins vs UPI: each is money but behaves differently. === is a strict shopkeeper who rejects a Rs.100 note photocopy — type must match exactly, unlike == which accepts lookalikes after conversion.
keyPoints: number covers integers and decimals (all 64-bit floats); use BigInt (10n) for huge integers.
string with quotes/backticks; boolean true/false; null (intentional empty) vs undefined (never assigned).
=== strict equality (no conversion) — always prefer it; == loose equality converts ("5" == 5 is true, a classic bug).
Arithmetic: + - * / % **; + with a string concatenates: "Age: " + 21.
Logical: && (and), || (or), ! (not); || and ?? (nullish) give defaults — ?? only falls back on null/undefined.
Convert explicitly: Number("42"), String(42), Boolean(0) is false; check NaN with Number.isNaN().

interview.question: == vs === — explain with an example.
interview.answer: == converts types first ("5" == 5 is true); === requires same type (5 === "5" is false). Teams enforce === (eslint eqeqeq) to kill conversion bugs.

interview.question: List all falsy values.

interview.question: null vs undefined?
interview.answer: undefined: declared but never assigned (or missing property); null: intentional "no value". typeof null is "object" (legacy bug); test null with === null.

interview.question: Why is NaN === NaN false?
interview.answer: NaN means "not a number result" and IEEE-754 defines it as unequal to everything including itself. Use Number.isNaN(x) to detect it.

topics.title: Conditions & loops
topics.definition: Conditions (if/else, switch, ternary) choose paths; loops (for, while, for...of) repeat work. Together they turn static scripts into programs that react to data.
topics.analogy: Like a festival food stall: if a customer pays, serve; else ask again. The cook repeats dosa after dosa (loop) until the batter ends, skipping burnt ones (continue) and stopping when the gas runs out (break).
keyPoints: if/else if/else picks the first true branch; switch matches one value against many cases (remember break).
Ternary cond ? a : b fits two-way choices in one line: status = marks >= 40 ? "pass" : "fail".
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) counts precisely; for...of walks array values directly.
while repeats while a test holds — always move toward the exit or it loops forever.
break exits the loop; continue skips to the next round; both pair with if inside loops.
Compare with === in conditions; == invites conversion bugs into every branch.

interview.question: for vs for...of vs forEach — which when?
interview.answer: Classic for: index control, break/continue. for...of: values, supports break/continue/await. forEach: concise but cannot break or await properly — avoid for async work.

interview.question: What happens if switch misses break?
interview.answer: Execution falls through into the next case body regardless of its label — sometimes intentional (stacked cases), usually a bug. Linters flag it.

interview.question: How do you avoid infinite while loops?
interview.answer: Guarantee progress toward the exit (counter/flag), cap iterations for safety, and prefer for/for...of when the bound is known upfront.

interview.question: == inside a condition - real danger example?
interview.answer: if (input == 0) is true for "", false, "0" too - any of those wrongly pass. === restricts to real zeros.

topics.title: Functions: declarations, arrows & scope
topics.definition: Functions package reusable steps: declare with function or const arrow, pass arguments, return a result. Scope decides where a name is visible - block scope (let/const) keeps variables inside their { }.
topics.analogy: Like a dosa counter with a fixed recipe card: you hand over batter and filling (arguments), the cook follows steps and returns a dosa (return value). The masala bowl stays inside the counter (scope) - the dining hall cannot grab it directly.
keyPoints: function greet(name) { return ...; } declares; greet("Asha") calls it with an argument.
Arrow functions: const add = (a, b) => a + b; - short form, great for callbacks.
return sends a value back and exits immediately; a function without return gives undefined.
let/const are block-scoped: visible only inside their { }; var leaks to the function - avoid it.
Default parameters fill gaps: function fee(age = 10) uses 10 when no age is passed.
Rest (...args) collects extra arguments into an array; spread (...arr) expands one.

interview.question: function vs arrow - real differences?
interview.answer: Arrows: shorter, no own this/arguments, cannot be constructors. Use arrows for callbacks; use function for methods needing this or hoisted helpers.

interview.question: What is scope and why does let beat var?
interview.answer: Scope is where a name is visible. let/const are block-scoped (each loop round gets its own); var is function-scoped and shared - the classic loop+setTimeout bug.

interview.question: What is a closure in one example?

interview.question: Rest vs spread - same dots, different jobs?

topics.title: Arrays & objects
topics.definition: Arrays store ordered lists (arr[0], .length, .push); objects store named properties ({name: "Asha"}). Array methods (map, filter, find) transform data without manual loops.
topics.analogy: Like a train pantry: the array is the numbered coach (berth 0, 1, 2 - order matters); the object is the labelled storage box (sugar jar, milk jar - names matter). map/filter are the pantry staff refilling every berth the same way.
keyPoints: Arrays: const a = [4, 8]; a[0] is 4; a.length is 2; a.push(9) appends.
Objects: const s = {name: "Asha"}; read with s.name or s["name"]; add with s.city = "Pune".
map builds a new array by transforming each item; filter keeps only matching items.
find returns the first match (or undefined); includes checks membership.
Spread [...a, 5] copies plus extras; destructure const [x, y] = pair.
Loop arrays with for...of; loop object keys with for...in or Object.entries().

interview.question: How do objects differ from arrays?

interview.question: Reference trap: const b = a; b.push(1)?

topics.title: DOM: selecting & changing the page
topics.definition: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the live tree of a web page. JavaScript selects nodes (querySelector), changes text, styles and classes, creates elements, and reacts to clicks and typing with event listeners.
topics.analogy: Like redecorating a shop display while customers watch: querySelector points at one shelf, textContent swaps the price board, classList toggles festival lights, and addEventListener rings the bell whenever someone touches the door.
keyPoints: document.querySelector(".price") picks the first match; querySelectorAll returns all matches as a list.
el.textContent sets safe plain text; innerHTML parses HTML (never feed it raw user input - XSS).
Toggle looks with el.classList.add/remove/toggle and el.style for one-off styles.
Create nodes with document.createElement, attach with parent.append, remove with el.remove().
el.addEventListener("click", fn) reacts to clicks; input events fire on every keystroke.
Put scripts at the end of body (or use defer) so the elements exist before your code runs.

interview.question: What is event delegation and why?
interview.answer: One parent listener handles child events via e.target. Survives re-renders, uses less memory, and needs no rebinding when items are added dynamically.

interview.question: Why does my script see null from querySelector?

topics.title: Spread, destructure & array methods
topics.definition: Modern JS transforms collections without manual loops: spread (...) copies and merges, destructuring unpacks values into names, and map/filter/reduce/find express the intent of each pass over an array.
topics.analogy: Like a mess manager handling thalis: spread copies the whole thali layout to a new plate, destructuring hands dal to one student and rice to another by name, and map/filter are assembly lines - one adds extra roti to every plate, one removes plates without dal.
keyPoints: Spread copies: [...a, 4] extends arrays; {...user, city: "Pune"} clones objects with one change.
Destructure to name things: const [first, second] = marks; const {name, city} = student.
map builds a new transformed array; the original is untouched (immutability wins in React).
filter keeps matches; find returns the first match (or undefined); some/every test the group.
reduce folds many values into one: sums, totals, grouped objects - start from an initial value.
Chaining (filter then map) reads like a pipeline; keep each step small and named when reused.

interview.question: map vs forEach vs for...of?
interview.answer: map returns a new transformed array (pure, chainable). forEach returns undefined - side effects only, cannot break. for...of supports break/continue/await. Default to map for transforms.

interview.question: Why spread instead of direct assignment?
interview.answer: Assignment copies the reference: two names, one array - mutating one surprises the other. Spread makes a real shallow copy so updates stay local.

interview.question: Shallow copy gotcha with nested objects?
interview.answer: Spread copies one level: nested objects still share references. {...user} then editing .address mutates the original - deep-clone (structuredClone) for nested edits.

interview.question: When is reduce the right tool?
interview.answer: Many values into one: sums, products, grouped lookups, frequency counts. If the result is still an array, map/filter express intent better.

topics.title: Async JS: promises, await & fetch
topics.definition: Async code waits without blocking: promises represent future values, .then chains steps, async/await writes waiting code flatly, and fetch() loads data from APIs over HTTP.
topics.analogy: Like ordering at a busy canteen: you take a token (promise) instead of blocking the counter; the kitchen calls your number when ready (.then); async/await is sitting down while the waiter brings each course in order; fetch is phoning the supplier for fresh stock.
keyPoints: Promise states: pending, fulfilled, rejected - .then handles success, .catch handles failure.
async functions always return promises; await pauses that function only, never the whole page.
fetch(url) returns a promise of Response; await (await fetch(url)).json() reads the body.
Promise.all runs jobs together (total time is the slowest); Promise.allSettled never short-circuits.
await in loops runs steps one by one (slow); map to promises + Promise.all runs them together.
Always handle rejection: try/catch around await or .catch at chain end, else silent failures.

lineByLine.explanation: Wraps the timer in a future value.
After 100ms the promise fulfils with result.
Runs when ready: prints dosa ready.

lineByLine.explanation: Async wrapper: lets us use await inside.

advancedExamples.code:

const data = await Promise.race([fetch("https://api.example.com/menu"), timeout(3000)]);
advancedExamples.note: race() takes the first settler: a slow API becomes a caught slow error instead of a hung page.

advancedExamples.title: Sequential vs parallel loop
advancedExamples.note: await inside the loop waits per item (3x time); map + all overlaps them. Classic interview answer.

practice.answer:

practice.answer: try { return await city(); } catch { return "Bengaluru"; }

practice.question: Fix: for loop with await get(id) is slow - why and fix?
practice.answer: await Promise.all(ids.map(get));

interview.question: What does await actually pause?
interview.answer: Only its own async function, freeing the event loop for other work. The rest of the page keeps running - that is why async I/O scales.

interview.question: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race?
interview.answer: all: all fulfil or first rejection wins. allSettled: waits for everything, reports per-status. race: first settler wins - ideal for timeouts.

interview.question: Why is await-in-loop usually a bug?
interview.answer: Each iteration waits fully before starting the next, serialising independent work. Map to promises first, then one Promise.all.

interview.question: How do unhandled rejections surface?
interview.answer: No .catch/try-catch means the rejection escapes: Node crashes workers, browsers log errors. Always terminate chains with handling.

topics.title: Events & forms
topics.definition: Events (click, submit, input) let pages react to users. addEventListener attaches a handler; the event object describes what happened; preventDefault stops the browser default like form reload.
topics.analogy: Like a shop doorbell: the bell (listener) waits quietly, each entering customer (event) rings it with details, and the keeper (handler) can hold the door shut (preventDefault) instead of letting it swing.
keyPoints: el.addEventListener("click", fn) attaches; removeEventListener detaches the same function.
Handlers receive an event object: e.target is what was acted on, e.preventDefault() stops defaults.
Form submit reloads unless you preventDefault - then read values from the inputs yourself.
input fires per keystroke (live search); change fires on commit (dropdowns, checkboxes).
Events bubble: a button click also fires parent handlers unless stopPropagation is called.
Delegate: one listener on a parent list beats hundreds on rows - e.target tells which child.

interview.question: Bubbling vs capturing - explain with an example?
interview.answer: Events travel down (capture) to the target then bubble up. A button click also triggers div handlers - use delegation deliberately, stopPropagation to contain.

interview.question: Why delegate instead of 100 listeners?
interview.answer: One parent listener plus e.target uses less memory, survives re-renders, and covers rows added later. The pattern behind every dynamic table.

interview.question: input vs change - which when?
interview.answer: input fires every keystroke (live preview); change fires on committed value (saving). Debounce input handlers that hit the network.

interview.question: What does preventDefault do - and not do?
interview.answer: Stops the browser default (reload, link jump). It does NOT stop other handlers - that is stopPropagation.

topics.title: Modules & tooling
topics.definition: Modules split code across files: export shares, import reuses. npm installs packages, package.json records them, and bundlers or Node run the result across environments.
topics.analogy: Like a thali kitchen with stations: each cook (module) exports finished dishes, the pass (import) collects them onto one thali, and the recipe book (package.json) lists every ingredient supplier (npm) so any branch rebuilds the same meal.
keyPoints: export function bill() shares; import { bill } from "./bill.js" reuses - names must match.
export default one main thing per file; import Bill from "./bill.js" names it freely.
Node needs "type": "module" for import syntax; browsers need <script type="module">.
npm install lodash fetches; package.json locks names, package-lock.json locks exact versions.
node app.js runs server code; the same module shape works in browsers via bundlers.
Never commit node_modules; npm ci rebuilds it exactly on any machine.

interview.question: Named vs default exports - team rule?
interview.answer: Named for libraries (many helpers, refactor-safe); default for one-main-thing components. Mixed files confuse - stay consistent per project.

interview.question: What do package.json and lock files each guarantee?
interview.answer: package.json: INTENT (names and ranges). lock: EXACT bits (every transitive version). Commit both; install with npm ci in CI.

interview.question: Why do circular imports break?
interview.answer: Each module executes once on first import; the circle re-enters half-ready bindings (undefined functions). Extract shared code to a third module.

interview.question: ESM vs CommonJS - practical differences?
interview.answer: ESM: static import/export, top-level await, browser-native. CJS: require/module.exports, dynamic, Node-legacy. Interop works but defaults and timing bite.

topics.title: Async: callbacks to promises to await
topics.definition: Async code waits without blocking: callbacks pass a done-function, promises hold future values with .then/.catch chains, async/await pauses inside an async function until the promise settles. The event loop keeps everything else running meanwhile.
topics.analogy: Like ordering at a busy dosa counter: callbacks are the boy shouting your name when ready; promises are the token slip you hold; async/await is sitting with the token - you pause YOUR journey, but the kitchen keeps cooking for everyone else.
keyPoints: Callbacks nest into callback hell past 2 levels - promises flatten them into chains.
A promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected exactly once; .then handles value, .catch errors.
async fn always returns a promise; await pauses THAT function until the promise settles.
Promise.all runs tasks together and fails fast; allSettled reports every outcome; race takes first.
await in for..of runs steps in order; Promise.all maps them in parallel - pick deliberately.
Unhandled rejections crash Node - always end chains with .catch or try/catch awaits.

interview.question: What does the event loop do with await?
interview.answer: await parks the async function and returns to the loop; when the promise settles, the function resumes from a microtask. Nothing blocks meanwhile.

interview.question: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race?
interview.answer: all: all values, fails fast. allSettled: every outcome, never rejects. race: first settler wins. any: first fulfiller wins.

interview.question: Why does async forEach drop work?
interview.answer: forEach fires callbacks and ignores returned promises - the loop ends before work finishes. Use for..of with await or Promise.all(map).

interview.question: Unhandled rejection - what happens?
interview.answer: Browser warns, Node crashes modern versions. End chains with .catch or wrap awaits in try/catch.

topics.title: Setup, compiler & first typed program
topics.definition: TypeScript (TS) is JavaScript plus static types. You write .ts files, the tsc compiler checks types and converts (transpiles) them to plain .js that runs anywhere JS runs.
topics.analogy: Like writing an address with a PIN code checker: JS delivers the letter anyway, TS verifies the PIN first so wrong addresses never leave your desk.
keyPoints: Install once: `npm install -g typescript`; check with `tsc --version`; start a project with `tsc --init`.
Compile with `tsc file.ts` (produces file.js), then run with `node file.js`.
Annotate with `: string`, `: number`, `: boolean`; the compiler rejects mismatches before runtime.
TS types vanish at runtime — they are a development-time safety net, not runtime checks.
`tsconfig.json` controls strictness; `"strict": true` is recommended for real projects.
Any valid JS is valid TS, so you can migrate file by file.

interview.question: What is TypeScript in one sentence, and where do types live?
interview.answer: A statically-typed superset of JS that compiles to plain JS; types exist only at compile time and are erased in the emitted JS.

interview.question: Why does `let x: number = "hi"` fail?
interview.answer: The compiler checks assignability: a string value is not assignable to a number-typed variable, so tsc reports error TS2322 before any code runs.

interview.question: What does strict mode add?
interview.answer: strictNullChecks (null/undefined are distinct types), noImplicitAny (every value needs a known type), plus checks on this, function types and property initialisation.

interview.question: If types are erased, how do you validate runtime data (e.g. API responses)?
interview.answer: Use runtime validators (Zod, io-ts) or manual guards — the compiler cannot check data that arrives after compilation.

topics.title: Core types: primitives, arrays & tuples
topics.definition: Core TS types: string, number, boolean, arrays (number[]), tuples ([string, number]), literal unions ("red" | "blue"), and enum-like unions. TS infers types from values, and widens/narrows them as code flows.
topics.analogy: Like railway ticket categories — Sleeper, 3AC, 2AC: each berth has a fixed category printed at booking (declaration), and the TTE (compiler) checks your ticket matches your coach.
keyPoints: string, number, boolean are the primitives; arrays as string[] or Array<string>.
Tuples fix length+order: let p: [string, number] = ["Asha", 92].
Literal types restrict to exact values: let dir: "L" | "R" = "L"; wrong strings fail compilation.
Inference: let city = "X" gives string automatically; const gives literal types.
any disables checking (avoid); unknown forces a check before use (prefer).
Type assertions (x as string) tell the compiler what you know — they add no runtime check.

interview.question: What does let city = "X" infer, and how does const differ?
interview.answer: let infers string (widened, reassignable); const infers the literal "X". Widening applies to mutable bindings so later assignments of other strings stay legal.

interview.question: any vs unknown — when is each acceptable?
interview.answer: unknown by default for untrusted data (forces narrowing); any only at system boundaries with a comment, or never — eslint bans explicit any.

interview.question: What is a tuple and when do you use one?
interview.answer: Fixed-length, ordered, heterogeneously-typed array ([string, number]). Use for pairs/coordinates/entries where position carries meaning; objects win for 3+ fields.

interview.question: Do assertions like `x as string` check anything at runtime?
interview.answer: No — purely compile-time. If x is actually a number, the lie compiles and fails at runtime. Prefer narrowing or validators (Zod) for runtime data.

topics.title: Unions & type narrowing
topics.definition: Union types (string | number) say a value may be one of several types. Narrowing — typeof, instanceof, in, truthiness checks — shrinks the union inside each branch so the compiler allows only safe operations.
topics.analogy: Like a railway platform announcement for "train OR bus passengers": the union boards everyone together, then narrowing checks tickets at each gate so metro riders take the metro stairs and bus riders take the bus exit.
keyPoints: Write unions with |: function printId(id: string | number) accepts either, rejects booleans.
Narrow with typeof x === "string" — inside the branch id is string, outside still the union.
Truthiness narrows too: if (name) removes "" | null | undefined from the type.
The in operator narrows object unions: if ("swim" in pet) picks the fish branch.
Literal unions ("up" | "down") plus exhaustive checks catch unhandled cases at compile time.
Optional chaining (?.) and ?? handle possibly-missing values without throwing.

interview.question: What is narrowing and why does TS need it?
interview.answer: Narrowing shrinks a union type inside a branch via checks (typeof, in, ===). Without it the compiler only allows operations valid for ALL members, so id.toUpperCase() on string | number is correctly rejected.

interview.question: in vs instanceof vs typeof — when each?
interview.answer: typeof: primitives. instanceof: class instances (Date, Error). in: object shapes by property. Truthiness: filtering null/undefined/empty.

interview.question: What is a discriminated union?
interview.answer: An object union sharing one literal field (kind/status) whose value identifies the shape. Switching on it narrows precisely — the backbone of typed API responses and state machines.

interview.question: ?. vs && chains, and ?? vs ||?
interview.answer: ?. short-circuits null/undefined access; && also skips other falsies. ?? falls back only on null/undefined; || on any falsy - so 0 and "" survive ??.

topics.title: Functions: signatures & overloads
topics.definition: TS functions carry type signatures: typed parameters and return types checked at compile time. Optional (?) and default parameters handle missing args; overloads describe one function with several call shapes.
topics.analogy: Like a railway booking counter with a rate card on the wall: the signature lists exactly which tickets (parameters) the clerk accepts and what receipt (return type) you get - wrong form, no ticket, before you even queue.
keyPoints: Annotate both ends: function add(a: number, b: number): number - compiler rejects add("x", 1).
Optional params need ?: function greet(name?: string) - inside, name is string | undefined.
Defaults fill gaps: function fee(age: number = 10): number uses 10 when omitted.
void means "returns nothing useful"; never means "never returns" (throws or loops forever).
Overloads list each accepted call shape above one implementation signature.
Arrow types look like (a: number) => number - the same shape function types use everywhere.

interview.question: Why annotate return types instead of letting TS infer?
interview.answer: Explicit returns document intent, catch body bugs early (returning undefined by accident), and keep .d.ts APIs stable when internals change.

interview.question: Optional (?) vs default (=) vs union-with-undefined?
interview.answer: ? omits the arg and narrows to T | undefined; = also supplies a value; explicit T | undefined forces callers to pass something (possibly undefined).

interview.question: What are overloads for?
interview.answer: One implementation, several precise call shapes - e.g. get(id: number) vs get(ids: number[]). Beats a loose union signature that loses the input-output link.

interview.question: void vs undefined vs never as return types?
interview.answer: void: caller ignores the result. undefined: the value undefined is returned. never: the function never returns (throws/infinite loop) - used for exhaustiveness.

topics.title: Interfaces & type aliases
topics.definition: Interfaces and type aliases name object shapes: interface Student { name: string; marks: number }. Implementations must supply every required property with matching types - checked before runtime.
topics.analogy: Like an admission form template: the interface prints the exact boxes (name, marks, city?) every applicant must fill. ? boxes are optional; the office (compiler) rejects forms with missing or wrong-type entries.
keyPoints: interface Student { name: string; marks: number } names a reusable object shape.
Properties with ? are optional: city?: string may be missing entirely.
readonly id: number prevents reassignment after creation - IDs should never change.
type aliases (type Point = {x: number}) also name shapes; interfaces extend cleaner.
Excess property checks reject unknown fields in literals - typos fail fast.
Functions can live in interfaces: greet(): string forces implementers to provide it.

Why does {name: 5} fail for interface {name: string}?
practice.answer: // const s: Student = { name: 5, marks: 1 }; // ERROR: number not assignable to string

interview.question: interface vs type - which when?
interview.answer: Interfaces: object shapes, extendable, better errors. type: unions, tuples, primitives, compositions. Teams use interface for objects, type for everything else.

interview.question: What does ? actually add to a property?
interview.answer: It adds undefined to the type AND allows omission. Readers must narrow (?? / if) before use - the compiler enforces it.

interview.question: readonly vs const?
interview.answer: readonly locks a PROPERTY after creation; const locks a BINDING. const obj still allows obj.field = x unless the field is readonly.

interview.question: Excess property checks - example?
interview.answer: { name: "A", markss: 1 } for Student errors on the typo markss - but only in fresh literals, not in prebuilt variables. Catches spelling bugs early.

topics.title: Generics: reusable type-safe code
topics.definition: Generics add type parameters (T, K) so one function, class or interface works for many types while staying fully checked. Write once, reuse safely everywhere.
topics.analogy: Like a tiffin dabba manufacturer with adjustable moulds: one mould (generic function) makes 250ml or 1-litre dabbas depending on the setting (type argument) - every box still comes out perfectly shaped, never a lid that almost fits.
keyPoints: Declare with angle brackets: function first<T>(items: T[]): T returns the same type it received.
The compiler infers T from the call: first(["a"]) gives string without writing first<string>.
Constrain with extends: function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T) works for strings and arrays.
Generic interfaces model containers: interface Box<T> { item: T; label: string }.
keyof T means any key name of T; T[K] is the value type at that key - the safe lookup pair.
Defaults (T = string) and multiple params <K, V> cover maps, caches and API wrappers.

interview.question: What problem do generics solve vs any?
interview.answer: any disables checking (typos pass silently); generics preserve the exact type through the function so misuse still fails compilation while code stays reusable.

interview.question: Explain T extends { length: number }.
interview.answer: A constraint: callers may use any type WITH a numeric length. The function can safely read .length; number or boolean arguments are rejected.

interview.question: keyof and indexed access T[K] - use case?
interview.answer: Type-safe property access: get(obj, key) only accepts real keys and returns the matching value type - powers form libraries and ORMs.

interview.question: When do you write the type argument explicitly?
interview.answer: Usually never (inference covers it), but needed when inference picks too narrow a type, e.g. wrap<string | null>(null), or for empty collections: [] as number[].

topics.title: Classes & object-oriented types
topics.definition: TypeScript classes bundle typed fields with methods: constructor builds state, access modifiers (public/private/readonly) guard it, implements checks shape contracts, and extends reuses behaviour through inheritance.
topics.analogy: Like a bank account counter: the class is the counter design, private balance is the locked cash drawer only staff touch, public deposit is the service window anyone may use, and a savings counter extends the base counter with interest.
keyPoints: Fields need types and values: balance = 0 infers number; declare name: string for clarity.
constructor(name: string) assigns readonly name once; readonly fields cannot be reassigned.
private hides internals (balance); public methods (deposit) are the safe doorway in.
implements Account checks the class honours a shape; the compiler rejects missing members.
extends reuses a base class; override replaces behaviour; super calls the parent version.
abstract classes define shared skeletons that only children can instantiate.

advancedExamples.note: Interfaces describe shapes; classes create values. instanceof narrows classes only - interfaces vanish at runtime.

practice.question: class Book: title, pages; isLong() for pages over 300.
Make balance private with a deposit guard.
Dog extends Animal overriding speak().
practice.hint: extends plus super for shared fields.

practice.question: Fix: assigning to readonly id after creation.

interview.question: private vs #private vs protected?
interview.answer: private is compile-time only (erased, still visible in JS). #x is runtime-hard private. protected allows children access. Interviews probe the compile-vs-runtime gap.

interview.question: When interface, when abstract class?
interview.answer: Interface: pure shape contracts, multiple allowed, zero runtime. Abstract class: shared implementation plus enforced skeleton, single inheritance. Prefer interfaces for data shapes.

interview.question: What are parameter properties?
interview.answer: constructor(private title: string) declares the field AND assigns it - shorthand for the common declare-then-assign pattern.

interview.question: Do types exist at runtime?
interview.answer: No - all annotations erase to plain JS. instanceof works on classes (real values) but never on interfaces; validate runtime data with guards or Zod.

topics.title: Utility types: Partial, Pick & Record
topics.definition: Utility types transform existing types: Partial makes fields optional, Pick/Omit select or drop keys, Record builds key-to-value maps, Readonly freezes, and ReturnType extracts a functions result type.
topics.analogy: Like thali customisation: Partial is make everything optional for a diet plate; Pick is full meals but only dal and rice; Omit is everything except onion; Record is the printed price chart mapping every item to its cost.
keyPoints: Partial<T> options-ifies every field: perfect for update payloads and config objects.
Pick<T, K> keeps listed keys; Omit<T, K> drops listed keys - mirror tools for views vs forms.
Record<K, V> maps a key union to values: Record<"veg" | "bill", number> price tables.
Readonly<T> blocks reassignment; Required<T> reverses Partial by demanding every field.
ReturnType<typeof fn> and Parameters<typeof fn> derive types from functions - single source of truth.
Compose them: Partial<Pick<Order, "dish" | "qty">> narrows then relaxes in one line.

lineByLine.explanation: patch may carry dish, price, both or neither.
Half an object now compiles legally.

basicExamples.title: Pick and Omit
Record price chart

lineByLine.explanation: Every key must map to a number - miss one and it errors.

guidedExamples.title: Readonly freeze
ReturnType reuse

lineByLine.explanation: Total follows the function even if its return changes.

advancedExamples.title: Compose Pick + Partial
advancedExamples.note: Pick narrows to editable fields, Partial relaxes them - the standard edit-form type in one line.

advancedExamples.title: Record with template keys
advancedExamples.note: Template literal keys generate families (stock-mum, stock-pnq) - typed without writing each by hand.

practice.question: Make an UpdateUser where name and city are optional.
practice.answer:
type User = { name: string; city: string };
type UpdateUser = Partial<User>;

practice.question: Build a role-to-permissions map for admin and viewer.
practice.answer: const p: Record<"admin" | "viewer", string[]> = { admin: ["all"], viewer: ["read"] };

practice.question: Strip password from a User type.
practice.answer: type Safe = Omit<User, "pass">;

practice.question: Why does Record<"a"|"b", number> reject {a: 1}?
practice.answer: { a: 1, b: 0 } // every listed key required

interview.question: When Partial, when Required?
interview.answer: Partial for patches/drafts where fields arrive over time; Required to re-demand everything (e.g. validating a draft became complete).

interview.question: Pick vs Omit - which is safer long-term?
interview.answer: Pick whitelists: new sensitive fields stay hidden by default. Omit blacklists: new fields leak until added. Prefer Pick for public shapes.

interview.question: What does Record guarantee?
interview.answer: Totality: every key in the union maps to a value, checked at compile time. Ideal for lookup tables, reducers and exhaustive configs.

interview.question: Why derive with ReturnType instead of repeating?
interview.answer: One source of truth: when the function signature changes, derived types follow automatically instead of drifting into lies.

topics.title: Async types: promises & errors
topics.definition: Async functions return Promise<T>: a future value of type T. await unwraps it; try/catch handles rejection. Promise.all runs independent calls together and keeps every result typed.
topics.analogy: Like ordering from three cloud kitchens at once: each ticket (Promise<Meal>) is a typed promise of food. await waits at your gate for one; Promise.all lays the full thali; a burnt dish (rejection) goes to the complaint counter (catch).
keyPoints: async function f(): Promise<number> must return a number; forgetting async breaks the contract.
await pauses only the function, never the whole page; wrap fallible calls in try.
Promise.all([a, b]) types as a [T1, T2] tuple - one failure rejects everything.
Promise.allSettled never rejects: inspect status, value and reason per call.
Catch errors as unknown, then narrow with instanceof Error before reading .message.
Promise.resolve(x) and reject(e) build settled promises for tests and adapters.

basicExamples.title: Typed async fetch

lineByLine.explanation: Bad status becomes a typed rejection.

basicExamples.title: try/catch with unknown

lineByLine.explanation: TS forces unknown - you must narrow.

basicExamples.title: Parallel pair

lineByLine.explanation: Result is a typed tuple, not any[].

guidedExamples.title: allSettled audit

lineByLine.explanation: One promise per id; none sinks the batch.
Narrows each result before touching value.

guidedExamples.title: Timeout race

lineByLine.explanation: Rejects after 2s if the API lags.

advancedExamples.title: Retry helper
advancedExamples.note: Generic retry preserves type T across attempts - reuse for every flaky call.

advancedExamples.title: Result wrapper
advancedExamples.note: Result<T> makes failure a VALUE the compiler tracks - callers handle both arms.

practice.question: Fetch two users in parallel; print both names.
safeDivide(a, b): Promise<number> rejecting on b = 0; catch returns 0.
Log pass or fail per id with allSettled.
practice.hint: Map ids to promises, inspect status.

practice.question: Add a 1s timeout to any Promise<number>.

interview.question: Why is catch(e: unknown) forced - not any?
interview.answer: any lets you read e.message unchecked and crash on thrown strings. unknown forces narrowing, so only real Errors yield messages.

interview.question: all vs allSettled vs race - pick each?
interview.answer: all: need every result, fail fast. allSettled: audit batches where partial failure is fine. race: first-wins timeouts.

interview.question: What does an async function actually return?
interview.answer: Always a Promise of the declared type. return 5 fulfils with 5; throw rejects. Callers must await or .then it.

interview.question: How do you keep async errors typed?
interview.answer: Throw Error subclasses or return Result<T> unions; narrow unknown in catch. Never let raw rejections cross module boundaries.

topics.title: Advanced types: conditionals & mapped types
topics.definition: Conditional types (T extends U ? X : Y) pick a type based on a relationship; mapped types ({ [K in keyof T]: ... }) transform every property; infer captures a piece of a matched pattern.
topics.analogy: Like a tiffin subscription that reshapes itself: hand it a steel dabba (a type) and it returns a dabba with every compartment relabelled (mapped type). Conditional types are the if-this-then-that rule; infer is the caterer noticing the chutney compartment always holds chutney without being told.
keyPoints: type IsStr<T> = T extends string ? 'yes' : 'no' is a type-level ternary, evaluated only at compile time.
Bare T distributes over unions: IsStr<string|number> becomes 'yes'|'no'. Wrap [T] to stop that.
Mapped type: type RO<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] } transforms each property.
Key remapping: [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K>}`]: () => T[K] renames keys to getX.
infer extracts a type: type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : never.
Template literal types build string unions: `${Method} /${Path}` from 'GET'|'POST'.

basicExamples.title: A first conditional type

lineByLine.explanation: A type-level ternary: if T fits string the result is the literal 'yes'.
Feeding string makes A the literal type 'yes'.

basicExamples.title: Mapped type: nullable fields

lineByLine.line: type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };
lineByLine.explanation: Walks every key K of T and unions each value with null.

lineByLine.line: const draft: Nullable<Product> = { id: 1, name: null, price: 99.5 };
lineByLine.explanation: name may now be null — great for draft records.

basicExamples.title: infer to unwrap a Promise

lineByLine.line: type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
lineByLine.explanation: If T is a Promise, capture its inner type as V and return it.
Promise<string> matches, so Value becomes string.

guidedExamples.title: Distributive conditional

lineByLine.line: type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
lineByLine.explanation: Bare T makes it distribute — each union member handled separately.
Result is string[] | number[], not (string | number)[].

guidedExamples.title: Key remapping with as

lineByLine.line: type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };
lineByLine.explanation: Mapped type renaming each key to getX/getY via template literal + as.
Object must provide the transformed keys getX and getY.

advancedExamples.title: Utility types are mapped types
advancedExamples.note: Partial, Readonly and Pick are exactly these three mapped types. Once you see it, inventing project-specific utility types feels natural.

advancedExamples.title: Template literal routes
advancedExamples.note: Template literal types generate string unions from other unions — the basis of typed HTTP clients. A typo like 'GET /user' fails at compile time.

practice.question: Write Unwrap<T> that returns the element type of T[], else never.
Make every property of a type readonly.
Extract the parameter types of a function as a tuple.
Why does string extends T stay unresolved?
practice.hint: Type parameter must be on the left.
practice.answer: With string fixed and T open, the relationship cannot be decided. Write T extends string so the compiler resolves it when a concrete T arrives.

interview.question: What are conditional types and when do you use them?
interview.answer: Types that resolve to one of two types based on a check (T extends U ? X : Y). Use them when a function's return type depends on its argument type, to unwrap types, and to build helper types that map or filter types.

interview.question: Explain distributivity with an example.
interview.answer: With a bare type parameter, a conditional distributes over unions: Box<T> = T extends any ? {v:T} : never; Box<string|number> becomes {v:string}|{v:number}. Wrap in [T] to disable distribution.

interview.question: infer — what problem does it solve?
interview.answer: It captures a type from inside a matched pattern: ReturnType<T> = T extends (...a:any)=>infer R ? R : never. Without infer you could detect a shape but not extract and reuse a piece of it.

interview.question: How are Partial, Readonly, Pick, Record implemented?
interview.answer: All are mapped types: Partial adds ?, Readonly adds readonly, Pick selects keys K, Record<K,V> is { [P in K]: V }. They show almost every utility type combines mapped types with keyof.

topics.title: Modules, tsconfig & tooling
topics.definition: Modules split code into files: export shares names, import brings them in. tsconfig.json configures the compiler (strict, target, module). Tooling (tsc --watch, bundlers, ESLint, source maps) turns many .ts files into one optimized .js bundle.
topics.analogy: Like a big Indian kitchen divided into stations — tandoor, curry, sweets. Each station exports finished dishes (export); the head chef imports what a menu needs (import). tsconfig is the recipe rulebook (how spicy, how fast); the bundler is the catering van that packs every station's output into one delivery crate.
keyPoints: Named exports/imports: export function fee(){} then import { fee } from './billing'; default export gives one main thing.
A .ts file with no import/export is a global script; add one export to make it a module with its own scope.
ES modules are native in browsers and Node; "type":"module" in package.json makes .js files ESM.
tsconfig essentials: strict (all safety checks), target (JS version), module (module system), outDir (build folder).
tsc compiles types away — the output is plain JS; source maps let you debug the original .ts.
ts-node / tsx run TS directly in Node; bundlers (Vite, esbuild) tree-shake unused code for smaller bundles.

basicExamples.title: Export and import

lineByLine.explanation: export makes fee visible to other files.
Named import pulls exactly those two names.

basicExamples.title: Default export

lineByLine.explanation: A file's single default export, named freely on import.
Default import needs no braces and any local name.

basicExamples.title: tsconfig.json

lineByLine.explanation: Turns on the full battery of type-safety checks.
Which JS features tsc may emit.

guidedExamples.title: Import types only

lineByLine.explanation: import type pulls only the type — erased at compile time.
A normal import for the runtime function.

guidedExamples.title: tsx runs TS directly

lineByLine.explanation: tsx strips types on the fly, great for scripts and servers during development.

advancedExamples.title: Path aliases for clean imports
advancedExamples.note: Path aliases keep imports readable in large projects; the bundler must be configured to understand the same alias.

advancedExamples.title: Declaration files for untyped packages
advancedExamples.note: When a package ships no types, a .d.ts declaration file describes its API so your code still type-checks. Better still, prefer packages with @types/* or built-in types.

practice.question: Split a total() function into its own file and import it.
Write a minimal strict tsconfig.json.
Import only the type of a value you never call at runtime.
Why does tsc output still run without TS installed?
practice.hint: Types are erased at compile time.
practice.answer: tsc removes every type annotation and emits standard JavaScript. The running program contains no TypeScript — only plain JS that any engine can execute.

interview.question: named vs default export — when each?
interview.answer: Named for most things (many per file, clear import names, better tree-shaking and refactor safety). Default when a file has one primary export (a React component, a class). Avoid mixing in one file.

interview.question: What does tsc actually do to types?
interview.answer: Erases them. TypeScript is a compile-time layer; tsc checks then strips annotations and emits plain JS. Types never reach runtime, so they cost nothing at execution.

interview.question: Why is strict mode recommended?
interview.answer: It enables strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny and more, catching null/undefined bugs and untyped values at compile time. Turning it off pushes those bugs to production where they crash.

interview.question: import type vs import — difference?
interview.answer: import type is guaranteed erased, never emits a runtime import; import may keep a real module load. Use import type for pure types and isolatedModules-friendly code.

topics.title: Project: typed mini app & best practices
topics.definition: This capstone combines types, generics, modules and async into a small typed app: a typed data layer, validation, an async loader and a couple of tests. Best practices — strict mode, small pure functions, no any — keep it maintainable.
topics.analogy: Like running a full tiffin service end to end: you define the menu types (the menu card), take orders through a validated form, cook each dish in its own small station (functions), and taste-test before packing (tests). The result is a tidy operation anyone can join mid-shift and understand.
keyPoints: Model the domain with types first; let the compiler catch missing fields before you write logic.
Prefer pure functions (same input, same output, no side effects) — they are trivial to test.
Ban any and unknown; narrow unknown at the boundary instead of pretending it is safe.
Async boundaries should return Promise<T> and handle errors with try/catch or a Result type.
Keep functions small and named for intent; the type of a function documents its contract.
A few focused unit tests beat manual clicking — they also serve as living documentation.

basicExamples.title: A typed data model

lineByLine.line: type Student = { id: number; name: string; marks: number };
lineByLine.explanation: The domain shape — every student has these fields.
Return type is a small union, so callers can switch on it safely.

lineByLine.line: const s: Student = { id: 1, name: 'Asha', marks: 92 };
lineByLine.explanation: A typed value; a missing field would not compile.

basicExamples.title: Pure function + test

lineByLine.explanation: Pure: depends only on its argument, returns a value.
Edge case: empty list returns 0, not a crash.

basicExamples.title: Validate unknown input

lineByLine.line: function isStudent(x: unknown): x is Student
lineByLine.explanation: A type guard: returns true and narrows x to Student.

guidedExamples.title: Async loader with error handling

lineByLine.line: type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string };
return { ok: false, error: 'failed to load' };
lineByLine.explanation: Errors become values, not thrown exceptions.

guidedExamples.title: Generic cache

lineByLine.explanation: Call fn once, then reuse — ??= assigns only if undefined.

advancedExamples.title: Type-safe event emitter
advancedExamples.note: keyof + mapped types give per-event payload types; a wrong handler fails at compile time.

advancedExamples.title: Small typed module boundary
advancedExamples.note: Keep types in one module and import type where needed — a clean, strict boundary between data and logic.

practice.question: Model a Product type and a pure priceWithGST(p) function.
Write a type guard isNumberArray(x: unknown) narrowing to number[].
Make an async fake fetch returning Promise<string>, await it in a function.
Why is `any` dangerous in a codebase? Replace with a safer option.
practice.hint: any disables all checks; use unknown + narrowing.

interview.question: How do you type a React/async API response safely?
interview.answer: Model it with a type/interface, treat the fetched JSON as unknown, then validate (type guard or Zod) before use. Never `as MyType` on raw fetch data — it lies at runtime.

interview.question: What are utility types and name three?
interview.answer: Helpers built on generics: Partial<T> (all optional), Pick<T,K> (subset), Omit<T,K> (exclude), Readonly<T>, Record<K,V>, ReturnType<F>. They reuse one type in many shapes without duplication.

interview.question: strictNullChecks — what breaks and why is it worth it?
interview.answer: null/undefined are no longer assignable everywhere, so you must handle them. It catches the classic "cannot read property of undefined" bugs at compile time instead of in production.

interview.question: How do you keep a growing TS project safe?
interview.answer: strict on, no any (lint rule), validate at boundaries, small typed modules with explicit exports, types close to domain, and unit tests on pure functions — the compiler then guards the rest.

languages.name: Java

topics.title: JDK setup & your first program
topics.definition: Java is a compiled, statically-typed, object-oriented language. You write .java files, javac compiles them to bytecode (.class), and the JVM (Java Virtual Machine) runs that bytecode anywhere.
topics.analogy: Like writing an exam answer sheet that any examiner in India can grade: javac converts your writing to a standard answer key (bytecode), and every JVM reads that key identically.
keyPoints: Install a JDK (17+ LTS recommended); verify with `java -version` and `javac -version`.
Every program lives in a class; execution starts at `public static void main(String[] args)`.
Compile: `javac Main.java`; run: `java Main` (no .class extension when running).
Java is statically typed: `int age = 19;` — the type is fixed at declaration.
Statements end with semicolons; { } braces define class and method blocks.

interview.question: Primitive vs reference types?
interview.answer: Primitives (int, boolean...) store values directly on the stack; references (String, objects) store an address to heap data. Copies of primitives are independent; copies of references share the object.

interview.question: Why does 7/2 give 3 in Java?

interview.question: == vs .equals() for Strings?

interview.question: What is `final` on a variable?
interview.answer: The binding cannot be reassigned after initialisation (constants by convention UPPER_CASE). For objects, the reference is fixed but contents may still mutate.

topics.title: Methods: params, return & overloading
topics.definition: Methods are named actions inside classes: static methods belong to the class, instance methods to objects. Parameters receive input, return sends a result; overloading reuses one name with different parameter lists.

Signature = name + parameter types; return type fixed (use void for nothing).
Overloading: same name, different params (area(5) vs area(5, 3)) - compiler picks by args.
Parameters pass by value: primitives copy; object references copy the address (contents shared).
return exits immediately with a value; every non-void path must return.
Helper methods should be small, named by intent (calculateBill), and static when stateless.

interview.question: static vs instance methods?
interview.answer: static belongs to the class (no object, no this); instance belongs to objects (has this, sees fields). Stateless helpers go static; behaviour needing object state goes instance.

interview.question: What is overloading and how is it resolved?
interview.answer: Same name, different parameter lists; the compiler picks the closest match at compile time. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.

interview.question: Java pass-by-value or reference?

interview.question: Can you overload by return type only?

interview.question: Class vs object vs reference?
interview.answer: Class is the blueprint; object is heap data built by new; the variable holds a reference (address) to it. Two variables can reference one object.

interview.question: What does a constructor do and not do?

interview.answer: Enables string-pool sharing, safe HashMap keys, and thread safety. Trade-off: edits allocate new objects, hence StringBuilder.

topics.title: Inheritance & polymorphism
topics.definition: Inheritance lets a child class reuse a parent class with extends; polymorphism lets child objects stand in for parent types, so one call runs the right override at runtime.
topics.analogy: Like a family sweet shop: the parent recipe (Mysore pak) passes to children, each adding a flavour (override). Customers order sweets by the family name (parent type) and each shop serves its own version - same order, different taste.
keyPoints: class Child extends Parent inherits fields and methods; super(...) calls the parent constructor first.
@Override replaces a parent method; the annotation makes typos a compile error instead of silent bugs.
A Parent-typed variable can hold any child: Payment p = new UpiPayment(); the child method runs.
final methods cannot be overridden; final classes cannot be extended; abstract methods must be overridden.
Constructors are NOT inherited - every child constructor must chain super(...) or this(...).
Prefer composition over deep hierarchies: more than 3 levels usually signals a design smell.

interview.question: Why is super(...) mandatory as the first line?
interview.answer: The parent part of the object must exist before child code touches it. Java enforces the order so inherited fields are never half-built.

topics.title: Interfaces, exceptions & packages
topics.definition: Interfaces declare capabilities (can-do contracts) that unrelated classes implement. Exceptions (try/catch/finally) handle failures without crashing; packages organise classes into namespaces.
topics.analogy: Like a driving licence: the RTO (interface) lists what any driver must do (start, stop) without caring which car (class) you bring. Exceptions are airbags - trouble triggers a controlled stop (catch) instead of a wreck. Packages are city zones keeping addresses unique.
keyPoints: interface Payable { int pay(int amt); } declares; class Upi implements Payable supplies the body.
A class implements many interfaces but extends one class - interfaces dodge the diamond problem.
try { risky(); } catch (IOException e) { } handles; finally always runs for cleanup.
Checked exceptions (IOException) must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked (NullPointer) need not.
throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad age") raises your own failures with clear messages.

interview.question: Abstract class vs interface - final answer?
