interview.question: Checked vs unchecked exceptions?
interview.answer: Checked (IOException): compiler forces handling - recoverable conditions. Unchecked (NullPointer): programming bugs, no forcing. Catching unchecked everywhere hides bugs.

interview.question: Why try-with-resources over finally close?

interview.question: What do packages solve?

topics.title: Collections & generics
topics.definition: The Collections Framework adds growable containers - List, Set, Map, Queue - with fast search, sorting and iteration. Generics (<T>) type those containers so the compiler rejects the wrong kind of element before you run.
topics.analogy: Like a South Indian kitchen shelf system: ArrayList is the open rack where you can push in another jar at any time; LinkedList is a chain of tiffin boxes hooked to each other; HashSet is the label-checked shelf that refuses a duplicate jar; HashMap is the sticker board that finds any jar by its written name instead of hunting shelf by shelf.
keyPoints: Declare with the interface and construct the class: List<String> n = new ArrayList<>(); - swap implementations later without touching callers.
ArrayList is the default: O(1) reads and appends. LinkedList only wins for heavy insert or remove in the middle.
HashMap gives O(1) lookup by key; TreeMap keeps keys sorted at O(log n) per operation.
Collections.sort, Collections.max and Collections.frequency do the common maths so you do not hand-write loops.
Override equals and hashCode together or a HashSet will silently store what look like duplicates.
Use record (Java 16+) for read-only data holders - it generates equals, hashCode and toString correctly for free.

interview.question: ArrayList vs LinkedList - which by default?
interview.answer: ArrayList nearly always: an array gives O(1) indexed reads and cache-friendly iteration. LinkedList only wins for frequent middle insert/remove, which is rare in practice.

interview.question: How does HashMap work internally?
interview.answer: key.hashCode() selects a bucket and equals() resolves collisions inside it. O(1) average; long buckets are treeified in Java 8+ to keep worst case O(log n).

interview.question: State the equals/hashCode contract.
interview.answer: Equal objects must return equal hash codes, and unequal objects should spread across buckets. Override one without the other and HashMap or HashSet silently misbehaves.

interview.question: Comparable vs Comparator?
interview.answer: Comparable defines the single natural order inside the class via compareTo. Comparator is an external reusable rule allowing many sort orders. Prefer Comparator for flexibility.

topics.title: Exceptions, try-with-resources & file I/O
topics.definition: Exceptions signal problems at runtime: checked ones (IOException) the compiler makes you handle, unchecked ones (NullPointerException) come from logic bugs. try/catch/finally handles them, try-with-resources closes files automatically, and java.nio.file reads and writes text.
topics.analogy: Like ordering food on a delivery app: try is placing the order, catch is the support call when the restaurant is closed (handled without crashing), finally is the wallet page you always pass through, and try-with-resources is the auto-refund - the app closes the payment session itself even if the order failed.
keyPoints: Throw for exceptional conditions, not for normal flow - exceptions are slow and hide the happy path.
catch the most specific exception first; catching Exception early makes later blocks unreachable.
Never swallow an exception with an empty catch - log it or rethrow so the failure stays visible.
try-with-resources (try (var w = Files.newBufferedWriter(p))) closes automatically, even on exception.
Read a whole file with Files.readString(path); write with Files.writeString(path, text).
Create your own exception by extending Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked) with a clear message.

advancedExamples.note: Rethrow with the original as the cause so the stack trace keeps the real origin - never lose the chain.

interview.question: Checked vs unchecked exceptions?
interview.answer: Checked extend Exception (IOException): compiler forces handling because the caller can reasonably recover. Unchecked extend RuntimeException (NPE, ClassCast): programming bugs to fix, not to catch everywhere.

interview.question: Why is an empty catch block dangerous?
interview.answer: It hides failures, so bugs surface far from their cause. At minimum log with context or rethrow; prefer handling or converting to a result value.

interview.question: What does try-with-resources guarantee?
interview.answer: Every AutoCloseable resource is closed in reverse order at block exit - normal or exceptional. It removes the manual finally-with-null-check boilerplate and the leak risk.

interview.question: finally vs return inside try?
interview.answer: finally runs before the method actually returns, so a return inside finally silently overrides the try return value. Avoid returns in finally - the classic interview trap.

topics.title: Lambdas, streams & Optional
topics.definition: Lambdas are compact functions passed as values; the Stream API pipes collections through filter, map, reduce and collect without explicit loops; Optional wraps a value that may be absent so you handle it explicitly.
topics.analogy: Like a water-filter plant on a farm canal: the canal is your List, each filter station is a stream stage (remove mud = filter, chlorinate = map), and the tank at the end is collect. Optional is the sealed bottle label that honestly says whether the bottle is full or empty instead of handing you a blank.
keyPoints: Lambda syntax: (a, b) -> a + b; method reference: String::length - shorter when a method already exists.
filter keeps matching elements, map transforms each one, forEach consumes, collect materialises a result.
Streams are lazy: nothing runs until a terminal op (collect, count, reduce), so filtered-out stages cost nothing.
Use primitive streams (IntStream) to avoid boxing overhead in hot numeric loops.
Optional: use map, filter, orElse instead of get(); returning null from a method defeats the whole point.
Do not modify a collection while streaming it (ConcurrentModificationException) - collect to a new list first.

interview.question: Why are lambdas not just syntax sugar for anonymous classes?
interview.answer: They compile to invokedynamic, giving a smaller memory footprint and correct this-scoping (no shadowed outer reference). They also cannot mutate locals - only effectively final ones.

interview.question: Intermediate vs terminal operations?
interview.answer: Intermediate (filter, map, sorted) are lazy and return a new stream; terminal (collect, count, forEach) triggers evaluation and closes the stream. Without a terminal op, nothing executes.

interview.question: map vs flatMap in one line each?
interview.answer: map: one element in, one out. flatMap: one element in, a stream out, flattened. Use flatMap for nested collections and Optional chains.

interview.question: Why avoid Optional.get()?
interview.answer: get() throws NoSuchElementException on empty - the same crash Optional was meant to prevent. Use orElse, orElseGet, or orElseThrow with a clear message.

topics.title: Modern Java: records, sealed types & pattern matching
topics.definition: Modern Java shrinks boilerplate: records are immutable data carriers in one line, sealed classes restrict who may extend them, and pattern matching (instanceof, switch) tests and destructures shapes directly.
topics.analogy: Like swapping hand-written paper bills for a printed GST invoice: a record is the pre-printed template (fields filled once, never edited), sealed is a fixed approved-vendor list, and pattern matching is the clerk who reads the invoice type and files it automatically.
keyPoints: record Point(int x, int y) auto-generates constructor, accessors x()/y(), equals, hashCode and toString.
Records are final and immutable by design - ideal for DTOs, API responses and map keys.
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square - the compiler knows every subtype that can exist.
Pattern matching for instanceof: if (o instanceof Circle c) tests AND binds c in one step.
switch expressions with case Circle c -> ... return a value and need no break; they can demand exhaustiveness.
Records cannot extend classes or add mutable fields - use classes when you need inheritance.

interview.question: Records vs classes - decision rule?
interview.answer: Records for immutable data (DTOs, config, keys, API models). Classes when you need inheritance, mutable state or rich behaviour.

interview.question: What does a record generate, and what may you add?
interview.answer: Constructor, accessors (x() not getX()), equals, hashCode, toString. You may add static members, extra constructors and validation; you may not add instance fields.

interview.question: sealed + pattern matching: real benefit?
interview.answer: Closed hierarchies let the compiler verify exhaustiveness, so adding a subtype breaks exactly the switches that must handle it - refactors become compile errors, not production bugs.

interview.question: switch expression vs switch statement?
interview.answer: Expression returns a value, uses -> , cannot fall through, and can be required exhaustive. Statement is the legacy form with break and fall-through.

topics.title: Databases, tables & your first query
topics.definition: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language for storing and asking questions of relational databases. Data lives in tables (rows + columns); you write queries and the database returns matching rows.
topics.analogy: Like a railway reservation register: each page is a table, each line a passenger row, each column (name, berth, train) an attribute. SQL is the clerk who finds exactly the rows you describe.
keyPoints: A database holds tables; a table has named columns with types (TEXT, INT, DATE) and rows of data.
Core verbs: SELECT (read), INSERT (add), UPDATE (change), DELETE (remove), CREATE TABLE (define).
Every query ends with a semicolon; keywords are case-insensitive but UPPER CASE is the convention.
Install PostgreSQL locally or practise in a browser (e.g. SQLite playground) — syntax here is PostgreSQL-style.
Never run UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE on real data — without it, every row changes.
NULL means unknown/missing, not zero or empty string; test with IS NULL, never = NULL.

interview.question: What is a relational database in one minute?
interview.answer: Data stored in related tables of rows and columns, with keys linking them (e.g. orders.student_id -> students.id), queried with SQL, with the engine enforcing types and constraints.

interview.question: SELECT * — when is it fine vs harmful?
interview.answer: Fine for quick exploration; harmful in app code because it fetches unneeded columns (slow, breaks when columns change). List explicit columns instead.

interview.question: What does NULL mean and how do you test it?
interview.answer: NULL is unknown/missing — comparisons with = return unknown, not true. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

interview.question: Why is DELETE without WHERE dangerous?
interview.answer: Without WHERE every row is deleted. Safe habit: run the SELECT version first, use transactions, and restrict permissions on production.

topics.title: SELECT, WHERE & sorting
topics.definition: SELECT reads data: choose columns, filter rows with WHERE, order with ORDER BY, limit with LIMIT. WHERE combines conditions with AND, OR, NOT and patterns with LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL.
topics.analogy: Like ordering at a darshini: SELECT dosa, coffee says what you want; WHERE chutney = extra filters the order; ORDER BY bill DESC sorts the queue richest-first; LIMIT 5 serves only five plates.
keyPoints: Basic shape: SELECT col1, col2 FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY col LIMIT n;
Comparison: = <> < > <= >=; combine with AND (both), OR (either), NOT (negate) — AND binds tighter than OR.
LIKE patterns: % any run of chars, _ one char: WHERE name LIKE 'A%' finds Asha/Arjun.
IN (a, b, c) and BETWEEN 80 AND 100 simplify range tests; IS NULL finds missing values.
ORDER BY marks DESC, name ASC sorts; LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5 paginates (page 2 of 5-per-page).
SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result.

basicExamples.title: Choose columns and filter
Sorting and limiting
basicExamples.code:
SELECT name, marks
FROM students
ORDER BY marks DESC
LIMIT 3;

lineByLine.explanation: Highest marks first (ASC would be lowest first).
Return just the top 3 rows — the class toppers.

guidedExamples.title: AND, OR, NOT

lineByLine.explanation: Either condition suffices: A-names plus struggling students.

guidedExamples.title: IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL

lineByLine.explanation: Finds students with no recorded marks.

guidedExamples.title: LIKE patterns and wildcards

lineByLine.explanation: % matches any run of characters: names starting with A.
The _ wildcard matches exactly one character.
Combine a leading % to match any prefix before the domain.

advancedExamples.title: Pagination that stays stable
advancedExamples.code:
SELECT id, name, marks
FROM students
ORDER BY marks DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;
advancedExamples.note: Always ORDER BY a unique column (id) with the sort key, or rows can shuffle between pages.

advancedExamples.title: Case-insensitive search (PostgreSQL)
advancedExamples.note: ILIKE is PostgreSQL’s case-insensitive LIKE; LOWER() works on every database.

practice.question: List all students scoring below 40 (need remedial class).
practice.answer: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks < 40;

practice.question: Find names starting with R, sorted A–Z.
practice.answer: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'R%' ORDER BY name ASC;

practice.question: Top 5 scorers with name and marks.
practice.answer: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 5;

practice.question: Students with marks 50–70 OR missing marks.
practice.answer: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (marks BETWEEN 50 AND 70) OR marks IS NULL;

interview.question: Walk me through logical query order vs written order.
interview.answer: Written: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT. Executed: FROM -> WHERE -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT. That is why WHERE cannot use SELECT aliases but ORDER BY can.

interview.question: LIKE vs ILIKE vs = ?
interview.answer: = exact match; LIKE pattern match (case-sensitive, % and _ wildcards); ILIKE case-insensitive LIKE (PostgreSQL). For indexed prefix searches, name LIKE 'Ab%' can still use a btree index.

interview.question: Why is `WHERE marks = NULL` always empty?
interview.answer: = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Use IS NULL. (Even NULL = NULL is not true.)

interview.question: AND/OR precedence trap — example?
interview.answer: WHERE a OR b AND c means a OR (b AND c). Always parenthesise mixed logic: WHERE (a OR b) AND c — interviewers love this bug.

topics.title: Aggregation: GROUP BY & HAVING
topics.definition: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) collapse many rows into one value. GROUP BY splits rows into buckets first (one result row per group); HAVING filters groups the way WHERE filters rows.
topics.analogy: Like a class teacher totalling marks: first sort answer sheets into subject piles (GROUP BY subject), then compute each pile average (AVG), and finally keep only piles averaging above 80 (HAVING) — piles, not individual sheets.
keyPoints: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(marks) skips NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT city) counts unique values.
GROUP BY city turns one row per student into one row per city with the aggregate beside it.
HAVING filters AFTER grouping (on aggregates); WHERE filters BEFORE grouping (on raw rows).
Mixing bare columns with aggregates without GROUP BY is an error in PostgreSQL — every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
NULLs are ignored by SUM/AVG/COUNT(col) — a student with no marks does not drag the average to zero.
Alias aggregates (AS avg_marks) and ORDER BY the alias for readable top-N reports.

basicExamples.title: Whole-table totals
basicExamples.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS students,
       AVG(marks) AS avg_marks,
       MAX(marks) AS topper
FROM students;

lineByLine.explanation: Counts every row including NULL-mark rows.
One result row summarising the whole table.

basicExamples.title: Average per city

lineByLine.explanation: city is the bucket label; AVG summarises the bucket.
One output row per distinct city.

basicExamples.title: Keep only strong groups
basicExamples.code:
SELECT city, AVG(marks) AS avg_marks
FROM students
GROUP BY city
HAVING AVG(marks) >= 80;

lineByLine.explanation: HAVING tests the group result — WHERE could not do this.

guidedExamples.title: WHERE vs HAVING together
guidedExamples.code:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM students
WHERE marks IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

guidedExamples.title: Conditional counting with CASE

lineByLine.line: SUM(CASE WHEN marks >= 40 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
lineByLine.explanation: Adds 1 per passing row: a filtered count.

advancedExamples.title: Top city per... actually rank groups
advancedExamples.code:
SELECT city, AVG(marks) AS avg_marks
FROM students
WHERE marks IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY avg_marks DESC
LIMIT 1;
advancedExamples.note: ORDER BY an aggregate alias + LIMIT 1 finds the champion group without any app code.

advancedExamples.title: Rollup grand total
advancedExamples.code:
SELECT COALESCE(city, 'ALL CITIES') AS city,
       AVG(marks) AS avg_marks
FROM students
GROUP BY ROLLUP (city);
advancedExamples.note: ROLLUP adds a super-row (city NULL) with the grand average — one query, detail plus total.

practice.question: Count students per grade band: A (90+), B (60+), else C.
practice.answer: SELECT CASE WHEN marks >= 90 THEN 'A' WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 'B' ELSE 'C' END AS band, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY 1;

practice.question: Cities with more than 3 students, highest count first.
practice.answer: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 ORDER BY n DESC;

practice.question: Pass percentage of the class in one row.
practice.hint: AVG of a 1/0 CASE gives a ratio.
practice.answer: SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN marks >= 40 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) * 100 AS pass_pct FROM students;

practice.question: Why does SELECT city, AVG(marks) without GROUP BY fail?
practice.hint: city is bare (many values) beside one aggregate — PostgreSQL rejects the mix.
practice.answer: -- Fix: add GROUP BY city so each city gets its own average row.

interview.question: WHERE vs HAVING — precise difference?
interview.answer: WHERE filters raw rows before grouping (cannot use aggregates); HAVING filters grouped rows after aggregation (uses aggregates). Wrong placement is a compile error or wrong numbers.

interview.question: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT col)?
interview.answer: * counts rows including NULLs; col skips NULLs in that column; DISTINCT col counts unique non-NULL values. Mixing them up silently changes reports.

interview.question: Why must bare columns appear in GROUP BY (Postgres)?
interview.answer: Each output row represents a group, so every non-aggregated column must be constant within the group — enforced by listing it in GROUP BY. MySQL’s lax mode picks arbitrary values instead.

interview.question: How do NULLs affect aggregates?
interview.answer: All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs. AVG over (90, NULL) is 90, not 45 - correct for "average of recorded marks", wrong if missing means zero (then COALESCE first).

topics.title: Joins: combining tables
topics.definition: Joins combine rows from two tables using a shared key: INNER keeps only matches, LEFT keeps every left row (filling NULLs), RIGHT the reverse, FULL both sides. ON states the matching rule.
topics.analogy: Like matching wedding RSVP cards to the guest list: INNER seats only guests with both card and list entry; LEFT lists every invited guest and marks who never replied (NULL); the ON rule is comparing names on both papers.
keyPoints: INNER JOIN keeps rows with a match on BOTH sides - the strict guest list.
LEFT JOIN keeps ALL left rows; missing right sides become NULL - find gaps with WHERE right.id IS NULL.
ON states the link (orders.student_id = students.id); USING(id) is the short form for same-named keys.
Alias tables (students s) to keep queries short: s.city reads better than students.city.
Joining without ON (comma join) multiplies every row with every row - a cross join explosion.
Filter joined rows with WHERE after the JOIN; pre-filter big tables in subqueries/CTEs for speed.

basicExamples.title: INNER JOIN orders to students

lineByLine.explanation: s is a short alias for students.

lineByLine.line: INNER JOIN orders o ON o.student_id = s.id;
lineByLine.explanation: Keeps only students who actually ordered.
Name from the left, item from the right.

basicExamples.title: LEFT JOIN finds the gaps
basicExamples.code:
SELECT s.name
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.student_id = s.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

lineByLine.explanation: Keeps EVERY student, order or not.
NULL means no matching order - these students never ordered.

basicExamples.title: Count orders per student
basicExamples.code:
SELECT s.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.name;

lineByLine.explanation: Students with zero orders stay in the list.
Counts matches; NULL sides count as 0.

guidedExamples.title: Self-join pairs

lineByLine.line: FROM students a JOIN students b
lineByLine.explanation: Same table twice with two aliases.
Links each junior to their senior.

guidedExamples.title: Multi-table chain
guidedExamples.code:
SELECT s.name, m.dish
FROM students s
JOIN orders o ON o.student_id = s.id
JOIN menu m ON m.id = o.menu_id;

lineByLine.line: JOIN menu m ON m.id = o.menu_id;
lineByLine.explanation: Second link: what each order contains.

advancedExamples.title: FULL JOIN reconciliation
advancedExamples.code:
SELECT COALESCE(s.name, g.name) AS who,
       CASE WHEN s.id IS NULL THEN 'guest only'
            WHEN g.id IS NULL THEN 'student only'
            ELSE 'both' END AS status
FROM students s
FULL JOIN guests g ON g.email = s.email;
advancedExamples.note: FULL JOIN keeps both sides - the standard reconcile-two-lists audit query.

advancedExamples.title: Anti-join with NOT EXISTS
advancedExamples.note: NOT EXISTS often beats LEFT JOIN + IS NULL on big tables - the optimiser stops at the first match.

practice.question: List each student with their order items (only orderers).
practice.answer: SELECT s.name, o.item FROM students s INNER JOIN orders o ON o.student_id = s.id;

practice.question: Find menu dishes nobody ordered.
practice.hint: LEFT JOIN menu to orders, keep NULLs.
practice.answer: SELECT m.dish FROM menu m LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.menu_id = m.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

practice.question: Count orders per city, including zero-order cities.
practice.hint: LEFT JOIN then GROUP BY city.
practice.answer: SELECT s.city, COUNT(o.id) FROM students s LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.city;

practice.question: What explodes when ON is forgotten?
practice.hint: Comma join = every row x every row.
practice.answer:
-- SELECT * FROM students, orders; -- cross join: N*M rows!
-- Always write the ON condition.

interview.question: INNER vs LEFT vs FULL - one-line each?
interview.answer: INNER: only matches. LEFT: all left rows + NULLs for misses. FULL: all rows from both + NULLs wherever unmatched. RIGHT mirrors LEFT.

interview.question: How do you find orphans (no match on the other side)?
interview.answer: LEFT JOIN then WHERE right.key IS NULL - or NOT EXISTS. The IS NULL test must target the nullable side.

interview.question: ON vs WHERE in a join?
interview.answer: ON defines how rows pair up (before grouping); WHERE filters the joined result after. For LEFT JOINs, moving a right-side filter from ON to WHERE silently converts it to INNER.

interview.question: Why is a missing ON catastrophic?
interview.answer: Without ON every left row pairs with every right row (cross join): 10k x 10k = 100M rows. Always alias and always write the join condition.

topics.title: Subqueries & CTEs
topics.definition: Subqueries nest one SELECT inside another (in WHERE or FROM); CTEs (WITH name AS (...)) name those blocks up front so the main query reads top-down. Both break big questions into named steps.
topics.analogy: Like preparing a wedding feast: a subquery is fetching masala mid-cooking (nested errand); a CTE is prepping all ingredient bowls first (WITH ...), labelled and lined up, so the final cooking reads cleanly.
keyPoints: Scalar subquery returns one value: WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students).
IN subqueries test membership: WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM orders).
FROM subqueries (derived tables) must be aliased: FROM (SELECT ...) AS t.
WITH city_avg AS (...) names a step once, then SELECT from it like a table.
CTEs chain: WITH a AS (...), b AS (... SELECT FROM a ...) builds pipelines.
EXISTS checks presence without returning data - fastest for yes/no questions.

basicExamples.title: Above-average students

lineByLine.explanation: Inner query computes one number first.
Outer keeps rows beating that number.

basicExamples.title: Students who ordered
First CTE

lineByLine.explanation: Names the average as a one-row table.
Main query reads like plain English.

guidedExamples.title: EXISTS check

lineByLine.explanation: True when at least one order row matches.
Inner query references the outer row.

guidedExamples.title: Chained CTEs

advancedExamples.title: Derived table with alias
advancedExamples.note: FROM subqueries MUST be aliased (AS t) - then filter and join them like tables.

advancedExamples.title: Top-N per group pattern
advancedExamples.note: Correlated scalar: each student vs THEIR city average - per-group champions without window functions.

practice.question: Students scoring above their city average.
practice.answer: SELECT name FROM students s WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students WHERE city = s.city);

practice.question: Dishes never ordered, using NOT IN.
practice.answer: SELECT dish FROM menu WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT menu_id FROM orders);

practice.question: Rewrite an IN query as a CTE.
practice.answer:
WITH orderers AS (SELECT DISTINCT student_id FROM orders)
SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM orderers);

practice.question: EXISTS vs IN with NULLs - which is safer?
practice.answer: -- NOT IN returns nothing if the list has NULL; EXISTS never has this bug.

interview.question: Subquery vs CTE vs temp table?
interview.answer: Subquery: inline, single-use. CTE: named, readable, chainable, same statement only. Temp table: persists for the session, indexable - for big multi-step jobs.

interview.question: Correlated vs non-correlated subqueries?
interview.answer: Non-correlated runs once (independent). Correlated references the outer row and runs per row - powerful (per-group comparisons) but costlier.

interview.question: Why does NOT IN misbehave with NULLs?
interview.answer: x NOT IN (1, NULL) is UNKNOWN, never TRUE - so zero rows return. Use NOT EXISTS or filter NULLs out of the list.

interview.question: Can a CTE be referenced twice? Cost?
interview.answer: Yes - but Postgres may execute it twice unless MATERIALIZED. For expensive CTEs reused often, prefer temp tables.

topics.title: Window functions: RANK & ROW_NUMBER
topics.definition: Window functions compute across rows related to the current row without collapsing them: ROW_NUMBER() numbers rows, RANK() ranks with gaps for ties, SUM() OVER gives running totals. OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) defines each rows window.
topics.analogy: Like a marathon results board: every runner keeps their own row, but RANK() writes their position beside them, PARTITION BY city gives per-city positions, and the running total column is the cumulative water-station count as they pass.
keyPoints: OVER () is the window: PARTITION BY splits into groups (like GROUP BY but rows survive); ORDER BY orders inside.
ROW_NUMBER() numbers 1,2,3 with no ties; RANK() gives ties the same number then skips (1,1,3).
Aggregates as windows (SUM(marks) OVER (PARTITION BY city)) add group context to every row.
LAG(marks) peeks at the previous row; LEAD(marks) peeks ahead - perfect for growth math.
Windows run AFTER WHERE/GROUP BY, so filter first, then number the survivors.
Always ORDER BY inside OVER for ranking functions - without it the order is undefined.

basicExamples.title: Number every student

lineByLine.explanation: All rows survive with positions attached.

basicExamples.title: Rank with ties

lineByLine.explanation: Two students at rank 1 push next to 3.

basicExamples.title: Per-city toppers

guidedExamples.title: Running total

lineByLine.explanation: Each row shows total so far.

guidedExamples.title: Compare with previous

lineByLine.explanation: Previous rows marks beside each row.

advancedExamples.title: Top 2 per city
advancedExamples.note: Rank inside a subquery, filter outside - windows cannot appear in WHERE directly.

advancedExamples.title: Growth vs class average
advancedExamples.note: AVG() OVER () broadcasts the class average onto every row for instant comparison.

practice.question: Number students by marks descending.
practice.answer: SELECT name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) FROM students;

practice.question: DENSE_RANK vs RANK on tied marks - show both.
practice.answer: SELECT name, marks, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) r, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) d FROM students;

practice.question: Running count of admissions in date order.
practice.hint: COUNT(*) OVER with ORDER BY date.
practice.answer: SELECT name, COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY admitted) AS running_n FROM students;

practice.question: Why is WHERE rank = 1 an error? Fix it.
practice.hint: Windows evaluate after WHERE; wrap in subquery.
practice.answer: SELECT * FROM (SELECT name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) r FROM students) t WHERE r = 1;

interview.question: GROUP BY vs PARTITION BY?
interview.answer: GROUP BY collapses each group to one row. PARTITION BY keeps every row and attaches the group computation beside it - detail plus context.

interview.question: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK?
interview.answer: ROW_NUMBER: unique 1,2,3,4. RANK: ties share, gaps follow (1,1,3). DENSE_RANK: ties share, no gaps (1,1,2). Pick by whether ties should skip positions.

interview.question: Why cannot windows sit in WHERE?
interview.answer: Logical order: WHERE filters before windows compute. Filtered rows would change rankings - so rank in a subquery/CTE, filter outside.

interview.question: LAG/LEAD default and use?
interview.answer: LAG(x) reads the previous row, LEAD(x) the next; both NULL at edges unless given a default. Core tools for period-over-period and sequence checks.

topics.title: Schema: CREATE, keys & normalization
topics.definition: Schema design shapes tables: CREATE TABLE defines columns and types, PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies rows, FOREIGN KEY links tables, NOT NULL/UNIQUE/DEFAULT/CHECK guard quality, and normalization removes redundancy.
topics.analogy: Like planning a school building: CREATE TABLE raises each classroom with fixed desk sizes (types); PRIMARY KEY is the roll number on every desk; FOREIGN KEY is the corridor connecting class to library records; normalization stops writing the full address on every single page.
keyPoints: CREATE TABLE students(id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, marks INT CHECK(marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100));
PRIMARY KEY: unique + never null, one per table; SERIAL/BIGSERIAL/IDENTITY auto-numbers it.
FOREIGN KEY (city_id) REFERENCES cities(id) keeps links valid - orphans rejected, deletes controlled.
UNIQUE blocks duplicates (emails); DEFAULT fills values (created_at DEFAULT now()); CHECK enforces rules.
1NF: atomic values, no lists in cells. 2NF/3NF: every fact lives in one place, linked by keys.
ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN / DROP COLUMN evolves schema; CREATE INDEX speeds lookups on filtered columns.

basicExamples.title: Create two linked tables

lineByLine.explanation: Parent table with unique city names.
Every student must point at a real city.

basicExamples.title: Constraints guard quality
Evolve with ALTER
basicExamples.code:
ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT;
ALTER TABLE students ADD CONSTRAINT uniq_email UNIQUE (email);

lineByLine.explanation: New nullable column: old rows get NULL.

guidedExamples.title: Normalization example

lineByLine.explanation: Rename a city in one row, all students follow.

guidedExamples.title: Index for speed
guidedExamples.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_students_city ON students (city_id);
SELECT * FROM students WHERE city_id = 3;

lineByLine.explanation: B-tree on city_id: lookups jump instead of scanning.
This filter now uses the index.

advancedExamples.title: ON DELETE behaviour
advancedExamples.note: CASCADE deletes child orders with the student; SET NULL keeps orders but clears the link; RESTRICT blocks the delete. Choose per business rule.

advancedExamples.title: Composite keys
advancedExamples.code: CREATE TABLE enrol (student_id INT, course_id INT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));
advancedExamples.note: Two columns together unique: same student can take many courses but never the same one twice.

practice.question: Create courses(id, title unique, fee default 0, fee non-negative).
practice.answer: CREATE TABLE courses (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, fee INT DEFAULT 0 CHECK (fee >= 0));

practice.question: Link enrolments to students with a foreign key.
practice.answer: student_id INT REFERENCES students(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

practice.question: Add a UNIQUE email column to existing students.
practice.answer: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN email TEXT UNIQUE;

practice.question: City name repeated in every student row - normalise it.
practice.answer: Move names to cities(id, name); keep city_id REFERENCES cities(id) in students.

interview.question: Primary vs foreign vs unique keys?
interview.answer: Primary: the tables identity (unique, not null, one). Foreign: a pointer into another tables primary, enforcing valid links. Unique: no-duplicates rule on non-identity data like emails.

interview.question: 1NF through 3NF in one minute?
interview.answer: 1NF: atomic cells, no repeating groups. 2NF: no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: no transitive dependencies - facts depend only on the key. Result: each fact stored once.

interview.question: When do you denormalise?
interview.answer: Read-heavy analytics where joins cost too much: store a computed total or copy a name. Accept slower writes and sync risk for faster reads.

interview.question: What does an index cost?
interview.answer: Faster reads on filtered/sorted columns, but slower writes (index updated per insert) plus disk space. Index foreign keys and WHERE columns, not everything.

topics.title: Data changes: INSERT, UPDATE & DELETE
topics.definition: DML writes data: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows, DELETE removes them. Every UPDATE and DELETE needs a WHERE clause, or the change hits the whole table.
topics.analogy: Like a hostel mess register: INSERT writes a new student line, UPDATE corrects a spelling in one named row, DELETE strikes a left student. Forgetting WHERE is spilling ink across every page at once.
keyPoints: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES (’Asha’, 92) adds one row; list columns explicitly.
Multi-row INSERT stacks tuples: VALUES (a), (b), (c) - one round trip for many rows.
UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 7 changes one row; without WHERE every row changes.
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 7 removes matches; TRUNCATE empties fast but keeps the table.
RETURNING id, marks shows affected rows immediately - no second SELECT needed.
Wrap related writes in a transaction so all succeed or all roll back together.

basicExamples.title: Insert one row

lineByLine.explanation: Shows the new auto-generated id at once.

basicExamples.title: Insert many rows
basicExamples.code:
INSERT INTO students (name, city, marks)
VALUES (’Asha’, ’Pune’, 92),
       (’Ravi’, ’Delhi’, 78),
       (’Meena’, ’Pune’, 85);

lineByLine.explanation: Far faster than three separate INSERTs.

basicExamples.title: Safe update
basicExamples.code:
UPDATE students
SET marks = 95
WHERE id = 7
RETURNING name, marks;

lineByLine.explanation: WITHOUT this line every student gets 95.

guidedExamples.title: Conditional raise
guidedExamples.code:
UPDATE students
SET marks = marks + 5
WHERE city = ’Pune’ AND marks < 90
RETURNING name, marks;

lineByLine.explanation: Updates from the old value, not a fixed number.

guidedExamples.title: Delete with backup select

lineByLine.explanation: Keeps a copy of what was removed.

advancedExamples.title: Upsert with ON CONFLICT
advancedExamples.code:
INSERT INTO students (id, name, marks)
VALUES (7, ’Ravi’, 80)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET marks = EXCLUDED.marks
RETURNING *;
advancedExamples.note: Insert-or-update in one atomic step - no check-then-insert race between two requests.

advancedExamples.title: Update from another table
advancedExamples.code:
UPDATE students s
SET city = c.new_city
FROM corrections c
WHERE s.name = c.name;
advancedExamples.note: Joins inside UPDATE: mass-fix cities from a corrections sheet in a single statement.

practice.question: Add yourself (name, city, marks) and see the new id.
Give every Mumbai student +3 marks, capped display at 100.
practice.answer:
UPDATE students
SET marks = marks + 3
WHERE city = ’Mumbai’
RETURNING name, marks;

practice.question: Remove students with NULL marks after previewing them.
practice.hint: SELECT first, then DELETE with IS NULL.
practice.answer:
SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks IS NULL;
DELETE FROM students WHERE marks IS NULL;

practice.question: What does UPDATE students SET marks = 0 do? Fix it.

interview.question: Why is WHERE on UPDATE/DELETE the most feared line?
interview.answer: Without it the change hits every row. Production rule: write WHERE first, preview with SELECT, then run inside a transaction.

interview.question: INSERT single vs multi-row vs COPY?
interview.answer: Single: simple writes. Multi-row VALUES: bulk seeds in one trip. COPY: lakh-row loads from files, fastest by far. Pick by scale.

interview.question: What does RETURNING buy you?
interview.answer: Affected rows come back instantly - new ids, changed values - with no second query and no race with other writers.

interview.question: UPDATE..FROM and upserts - when?
interview.answer: UPDATE..FROM mass-fixes from another table; ON CONFLICT upserts make retries and syncs idempotent. Both keep multi-step logic inside one atomic statement.

topics.title: Transactions, isolation levels & locking
topics.definition: A transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit (BEGIN ... COMMIT / ROLLBACK). Isolation levels decide which effects of concurrent transactions are visible, trading consistency against speed.
topics.analogy: Like a bank cashier counter: a transaction serves one customer completely (check balance, deduct, print slip) - if any step fails nothing is applied. Isolation is how loudly the next customer can overhear the work in progress.
keyPoints: BEGIN ... COMMIT saves everything; ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN.
ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (survives crashes).
Isolation: READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads) < REPEATABLE READ (no non-repeatable reads) < SERIALIZABLE (no phantoms).
Dirty read: seeing uncommitted data. Non-repeatable read: the same row changes mid-transaction. Phantom: new rows appear in a re-run range query.
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ raises safety but adds blocking and deadlocks.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks chosen rows so two clerks cannot sell the same seat at once.
SAVEPOINT allows a partial rollback inside one transaction.

basicExamples.title: All-or-nothing transfer
ROLLBACK on error

lineByLine.explanation: Shows the ORIGINAL quantity - nothing applied.

basicExamples.title: Row lock for seat booking

lineByLine.explanation: Locks these rows; other writers WAIT here.
Safe because nobody else can change the row meanwhile.

guidedExamples.title: SAVEPOINT partial rollback

lineByLine.explanation: Undoes payments but KEEPS the order insert.

guidedExamples.title: Dirty read prevented

lineByLine.line: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

lineByLine.explanation: The change stays private until COMMIT.

lineByLine.line: -- Session B sees the OLD score
lineByLine.explanation: Uncommitted work is never visible to others.

advancedExamples.title: Idempotent upsert
advancedExamples.note: ON CONFLICT turns a duplicate-key crash into an increment - safe to retry sync jobs without double-counting.

advancedExamples.title: Deadlock-aware batch update
advancedExamples.note: Locking rows in one consistent ORDER prevents circular waits: clerk 1 does A-then-B while clerk 2 does B-then-A - the classic deadlock.

practice.question: Wrap two related inserts in one transaction with a savepoint.
Read the balance while locking the row for an update.
Explain phantom read with an example.
practice.hint: A range re-query returns extra rows mid-transaction.

practice.question: Why is REPEATABLE READ slower than READ COMMITTED?
practice.hint: It keeps snapshots/older row versions to guarantee identical re-reads.
practice.answer: Extra version storage plus more conflict checks mean more blocking and more deadlocks to retry.

interview.question: Define ACID precisely.
interview.answer: Atomicity: partial failure undoes all. Consistency: every constraint still holds after commit. Isolation: concurrent transactions behave as if serialised (per level). Durability: committed data survives a crash.

interview.question: Dirty vs non-repeatable vs phantom read?
interview.answer: Dirty: reading uncommitted data. Non-repeatable: the same row changed between two reads in one transaction. Phantom: a range re-query returns newly committed rows.

interview.question: FOR UPDATE vs FOR SHARE?
interview.answer: FOR UPDATE takes an exclusive lock - others cannot update or lock conflicting. FOR SHARE allows concurrent reads but blocks writers.

interview.question: How do you reduce deadlocks?
interview.answer: Lock rows in one consistent order, keep transactions short, touch the fewest rows needed, add indexes so locks do not escalate, and retry deadlock errors with backoff.

topics.title: Indexes, EXPLAIN & query performance
topics.definition: An index is an extra lookup structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the real plan and timing so you can prove a change helped.
topics.analogy: Like the index pages at the back of a textbook: instead of reading all 800 pages to find Kanyakumari you jump straight there. EXPLAIN is the librarian telling you which path they walked and how long each step took.
keyPoints: CREATE INDEX ON students (city); speeds lookups on city; UNIQUE INDEX also enforces uniqueness.
Indexes speed up WHERE, JOIN conditions and ORDER BY - but every write must maintain them too.
EXPLAIN shows the plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and reports real timings and row counts.
Seq Scan = full table read (fine for small tables); Index Scan / Index Only Scan = targeted lookup.
A huge gap between estimated and actual rows usually means stale statistics - run ANALYZE.
Composite index order matters: (city, marks) serves city and city+marks, but not marks alone.
A partial index (WHERE ...) is smaller and only covers the rows you actually query.

basicExamples.title: Create and verify an index
basicExamples.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_students_city ON students (city);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = 'Pune';

lineByLine.explanation: Builds a lookup structure on city.
Prints the plan without running it.
Index Scan = index used; Seq Scan = table scanned.

basicExamples.title: Composite index order

lineByLine.explanation: Leftmost column first - like surname then first name.
Both columns are served by this one index.
Would NOT use it - the leftmost column is missing.

basicExamples.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE real timings
basicExamples.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT city, AVG(marks) FROM students
WHERE marks IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY city;

lineByLine.explanation: Actually executes and reports milliseconds per node.
Watch for a Sort or HashAggregate node.
The numbers prove whether the index helped.

guidedExamples.title: Partial index for hot queries

lineByLine.explanation: The index stores only the rows you actually search.
Fits in memory, faster scans, cheaper maintenance.
Pending/failed/active rows are usually a small subset.

guidedExamples.title: Covering index avoids table hits
guidedExamples.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_cov ON students (city) INCLUDE (marks);
SELECT city, marks FROM students WHERE city = 'Pune';

lineByLine.explanation: Extra columns stored in the index leaves.
All needed data is in the index - table never touched.
Bigger index, but dramatically faster narrow reads.

advancedExamples.title: Fix the classic anti-pattern
advancedExamples.note: Any function wrapped around a column makes a plain index unusable - index the exact expression instead.

advancedExamples.title: Pagination without OFFSET slowdown
advancedExamples.code:
SELECT * FROM students
WHERE (marks, id) < (80, 5000)
ORDER BY marks DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
advancedExamples.note: OFFSET 100000 still walks 100000 rows. Keyset pagination on (marks, id) resumes exactly where the last page stopped.

practice.question: Add an index for lookups by email and enforce uniqueness.
practice.answer: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);

practice.question: Which index helps WHERE city = ? AND marks > ? but not marks alone?
practice.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_city_marks ON students (city, marks);

practice.question: EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan on a 1M-row table - what does it suggest?
practice.hint: No usable index for that predicate.
practice.answer: Add an index matching the WHERE columns, then re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare.

practice.question: Why does LIKE '%sha' not use an index?
practice.hint: A leading wildcard cannot bound the B-tree range.
practice.answer: Use a trigram index (pg_trgm) or full-text search for substring matching.

interview.question: What is an index and what does it cost?
interview.answer: A separate lookup structure (B-tree) enabling fast row location. Cost: extra disk space and slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE because every write maintains it.

interview.question: Index Scan vs Seq Scan vs Index Only Scan?
interview.answer: Seq Scan reads every row (fine for small tables). Index Scan finds rows via the index then fetches the table. Index Only Scan answers from the index alone - fastest.

interview.question: Why is composite index order critical?
interview.answer: It is a sorted structure: (a, b) can satisfy a and a+b but not b alone. Put equality/leftmost filters first, ranges last.

interview.question: How do you prove a query got faster?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after, comparing total time, rows removed by filter, and node types - never guess.

topics.title: Views, procedures & user-defined functions
topics.definition: A view is a saved named query that behaves like a read-only table. Stored procedures and user-defined functions package multi-statement logic inside the database so many applications share one tested implementation.
topics.analogy: Like a pre-mixed masala packet in a Kirana shop: instead of every home grinding the same spice mix, the shop prepares it once (CREATE VIEW / CREATE FUNCTION) and everyone just uses the packet by name. A procedure is the restaurant kitchen - you call "make thali" and many hidden steps run in order.
keyPoints: CREATE VIEW active_users AS SELECT ... saves the query; SELECT * FROM active_users then works like any table.
Views do not store data by default (Postgres evaluates the underlying query each time) - excellent for consistent definitions and column hiding.
Materialized views (Postgres) DO cache results - refresh them with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW after data changes.
CREATE FUNCTION f(a int) RETURNS int AS $$ ... $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql lets SQL call reusable logic; RETURNS TABLE returns rows.
GRANT column-level privileges on the base table, then expose only safe columns through the view for security.
ALTER VIEW / DROP VIEW manage them; views can be layered (a view on a view) but keep nesting shallow for debuggability.

basicExamples.title: Create and use a view

lineByLine.explanation: Saves this query under a name.
The definition - only passing rows are visible.
Queries the view exactly like a table.

basicExamples.title: A scalar function

lineByLine.line: CREATE FUNCTION grade_of(marks int) RETURNS char AS $$
lineByLine.explanation: One integer in, one character out.
The logic lives in the database, not in every app.

guidedExamples.title: Aggregating view for reports

lineByLine.explanation: Encapsulates a GROUP BY as a reusable report.
Filters on the aggregated result afterwards.

guidedExamples.title: A function returning a table

lineByLine.explanation: Takes the cut-off as a parameter.
Returns rows, not a single value.

guidedExamples.title: DROP safely with IF EXISTS

lineByLine.explanation: Removes the view; IF EXISTS prevents an error if it is already gone.
Functions are dropped by signature, not just name.
Same safety pattern for tables - re-runnable migration scripts.

advancedExamples.title: Materialized view for dashboards
advancedExamples.note: Caching a heavy aggregate turns a 30-second dashboard query into milliseconds; CONCURRENTLY allows reads during refresh.

advancedExamples.title: View for column-level security
advancedExamples.note: The app role can never read password_hash - the base table is simply not exposed. Security enforced in the schema, not in app code.

practice.question: Create a view of students above 80 marks, ordered by name.
practice.hint: CREATE VIEW with ORDER BY inside.
practice.answer: CREATE VIEW toppers AS SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 80 ORDER BY name;

practice.question: Write a function that returns the count of students in a city.
Hide the phone column from an app using a view.
practice.hint: Select only the safe columns; revoke base access.
practice.answer: CREATE VIEW safe_customers AS SELECT id, name, city FROM customers;

practice.question: Why is a plain view slow on a big aggregation? Fix it.
practice.hint: Views re-run the query; cache it instead.
practice.answer:
-- Use a materialized view + index:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW city_stats AS SELECT city, AVG(marks) a FROM students GROUP BY city;

interview.question: View vs materialized view?
interview.answer: A view stores only the query definition and re-evaluates on every use (always fresh, cost each time). A materialized view stores the RESULT set (fast reads, stale until refreshed). Pick by freshness vs speed.

interview.question: Are views updatable?
interview.answer: Simple single-table views without aggregates, DISTINCT or GROUP BY often are (INSERT/UPDATE pass through to the base table). Complex views need INSTEAD OF triggers. Views are primarily a read abstraction.

interview.question: Function vs procedure in Postgres?
interview.answer: Older Postgres only had functions; procedures (CREATE PROCEDURE) arrived in v11 and can COMMIT inside themselves. Functions cannot run transaction control, procedures can.

interview.question: Name three reasons to use views in a real system.
interview.answer: 1) Consistent business definitions shared by all apps. 2) Column-level security (hide password_hash/PII). 3) Backward-compatible schema evolution - reshape columns in a view instead of breaking clients.

topics.title: Analytics: pivots, cohorts & running totals
topics.definition: Analytical SQL answers "how did things change over time" questions: CASE pivots rows into columns, FILTER attaches conditions to aggregates, and window functions produce running totals, month-over-month growth and retention cohorts.
topics.analogy: Like a school annual report: a pivot turns the long attendance register (one row per student per day) into a compact table with a column for each month. A running total is the cumulative fees-collected tally, and a cohort is tracking the whole batch of 2025 students together instead of comparing every student to the school average.
keyPoints: Pivot pattern: SUM(CASE WHEN month = 1 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS jan - one column per bucket.
FILTER is the tidier Postgres form: SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE month = 1) AS jan.
Running total: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY d) - the frame grows to the current row.
Month-over-month growth needs LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY d) to reach the previous row.
Retention cohorts group users by signup month, then measure how many return in later months.
DATE_TRUNC('month', d) buckets timestamps; generate_series() fills gaps so missing months still appear.

basicExamples.title: Pivot months into columns
basicExamples.code:
SELECT city,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = 1 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS jan,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = 2 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS feb
FROM sales
GROUP BY city;

lineByLine.line: SUM(CASE WHEN month = 1 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS jan
lineByLine.explanation: Sums only January values into its own column.
Rows become cities, months become columns.

basicExamples.title: FILTER instead of CASE
basicExamples.code:
SELECT
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 90) AS a_grades,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE marks >= 60) AS b_or_above,
    COUNT(*) AS total
FROM students;

lineByLine.explanation: Same as the CASE version but reads far cleaner.
All columns computed in one pass.

basicExamples.title: Running total

lineByLine.explanation: Default frame: unbounded preceding to current row.
Each row shows the total earned so far.

guidedExamples.title: Month-over-month growth
guidedExamples.code:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS m, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT m, total,
       LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS prev,
       ROUND((total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY m)) * 100.0
             / NULLIF(LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY m), 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly;

lineByLine.line: LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS prev

lineByLine.explanation: Prevents division by zero on the first month.

guidedExamples.title: Fill missing months
guidedExamples.code:
SELECT m.month,
       COALESCE(s.total, 0) AS total
FROM generate_series('2026-01-01'::date, '2026-12-01'::date, '1 month') AS m(month)
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS mo, SUM(amount) total
           FROM orders GROUP BY 1) s ON s.mo = m.month;

lineByLine.explanation: Generates every month in the year.
Attaches real sales; missing months stay NULL.
Shows zero instead of blank gaps.

advancedExamples.title: Signup retention cohort
advancedExamples.code:
WITH first_seen AS (
    SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date)) AS cohort
    FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT f.cohort,
       DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS active_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS users
FROM first_seen f
JOIN orders o USING (user_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rnk
FROM sales;

  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE month = 2) AS feb,
  SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE month = 3) AS mar
FROM sales GROUP BY city;

practice.answer: SELECT name, marks, SUM(marks) OVER (ORDER BY marks) AS running FROM students;

practice.question: Show each city share of total sales as a percentage.
practice.answer: SELECT city, ROUND(SUM(amount) * 100.0 / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (), 2) AS pct FROM sales GROUP BY city;

practice.question: Compute month-over-month growth safely.

WITH m AS (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', d) mo, SUM(a) t FROM s GROUP BY 1)

interview.question: How do you pivot rows to columns in standard SQL?
interview.answer: Conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE WHEN bucket = x THEN value END) - one such expression per target column, plus GROUP BY the row dimension. FILTER is the Postgres shorthand.

interview.question: Running total vs running average - what changes?
interview.answer: Same OVER (ORDER BY ...) frame; swap SUM for AVG. The default frame grows to the current row, which is what makes it running rather than overall.

interview.question: Why does a LEFT JOIN on generate_series beat a self-join?
interview.answer: It guarantees every period appears even with zero sales - self-joins can only produce periods that already exist in the data. Charts need the zeros.

interview.question: What is a cohort analysis and why not just average everything?
interview.answer: Averages hide behaviour differences between signup periods. Cohorts track each signup month separately, revealing retention decay - a flat overall average can conceal a failing product.

topics.title: Toolchain, modules & first program
topics.definition: Go (Golang) is a compiled, statically-typed language from Google. You write .go files, organise them in modules, and `go run` / `go build` compiles them to a single fast binary.
topics.analogy: Like a tiffin delivery service with one sealed dabba: Go packs your whole program (all dependencies) into a single binary lunchbox that runs anywhere without extra setup.
keyPoints: Install Go from go.dev; verify with `go version`; every project starts with `go mod init example.com/hello`.
Every program has `package main` and `func main()` — execution starts there.
Run instantly: `go run .`; ship: `go build -o app .` then `./app`.
Declare with `var name string = "Asha"` or short `name := "Asha"` (inside functions only); types are fixed.
Import standard packages (fmt, strings); unused imports or variables are compile errors — delete or use them.
Format with `gofmt` / `go fmt ./...`; the compiler enforces braces on the same line as the statement.

	marks := 91.5
	passed := true
	fmt.Println(city, year, marks, passed)
	fmt.Printf("%T %T
", city, year)
}

interview.question: How does Go build and run code?
interview.answer: go run compiles to a temp binary and executes it; go build produces a standalone binary with dependencies included — no JVM/VM needed at runtime.

interview.question: := vs var — what is the difference?
interview.answer: := is shorthand inside functions only, inferring the type; var works at any scope and allows explicit types. Both create fixed-type variables.

interview.answer: Deliberate design: it keeps codebases clean and catches half-finished edits. Use the value, delete it, or assign to _ .

interview.question: What is a Go module?
interview.answer: A versioned collection of packages rooted at go.mod (module path + Go version + dependencies); go mod tidy keeps it consistent.

topics.title: Variables, types & operators
topics.definition: Go variables have fixed types set at declaration: integers (int), floats (float64), strings, booleans. Operators (+, -, *, /, %, ==, &&, ||, !) compute and compare; := declares with inference inside functions, var declares anywhere with optional explicit types.
topics.analogy: Like fixed-size steel lunch boxes: an int dabba holds only whole rotis, a string dabba only chits. := is the vendor guessing the box size from what you put in; var with a type is you ordering the exact size. The compiler rejects a soup box labelled rice.
keyPoints: Core types: int, float64, string, bool; check a value’s type with %T in fmt.Printf.
:= infers and declares inside functions only; var works at package level and allows explicit types.
Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 is 3; use 7.0 / 2 for 3.5.
Zero values: 0, 0.0, "", false — every variable starts useful, never garbage.
Convert explicitly: int(3.9) truncates to 3; string(65) gives "A" (rune!), use strconv.Itoa for digits.
Constants with const (and iota for sequences) can never change; unused variables/imports fail the build.

interview.question: What is a zero value and why does it matter?

topics.title: Control flow: if, for & switch
topics.definition: Go chooses with if/else, repeats ONLY with for (no while keyword - for covers it), and branches on values with switch. Short init statements (if x := f(); x > 0) keep conditions tidy.
topics.analogy: Like a Mumbai local: if the fast train comes take it else take slow (if/else); the motorman repeats stations with one loop handle (for does all looping); switch is the platform indicator routing each train number to its line.
keyPoints: if needs no parens but needs braces: if age >= 18 { ... } else { ... }.
for is the ONLY loop: for i := 0; i < 5; i++ counts; for cond { } acts as while.
for range walks collections: for i, v := range items gives index and value.
break exits, continue skips; switch matches values with implicit breaks (no fallthrough by default).
Init statement: if n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); err != nil { ... } scopes n to the branch.
++ and -- are statements, not expressions: x := i++ is illegal in Go.

interview.question: Why does Go have only for and no while?
interview.answer: One loop construct covers counting, conditionals (for cond), infinite (for {}), and ranging - fewer keywords, one idiom to master. for cond IS while.

interview.question: switch without fallthrough - explain.
interview.answer: Cases break automatically, unlike C. Explicit fallthrough keyword exists for the rare intentional cascade - the safe default.

interview.question: range gives what for slices vs maps?
interview.answer: Slices: index + copy of value. Maps: key + value in RANDOM order - never rely on map order. Use for i := range s when only the index matters.

interview.question: Init statements in if/switch - why idiomatic?
interview.answer: if x := f(); x > 0 keeps x scoped to the branches - no leaking temporaries, and err-checking reads as one thought.

topics.title: Collections: slices, maps & structs
topics.definition: Go collections: slices are growable views over arrays (append, len, cap), maps are key-value lookups (make, delete, comma-ok), structs bundle named fields into one record type.
topics.analogy: Like a wedding guest system: slices are the flexible seating rows (add chairs with append), maps are the name-to-table lookup register, and structs are the per-guest card holding name, table and food choice together.
keyPoints: Slices: s := []int{1,2}; s = append(s, 3); len(s) counts used, cap(s) counts room.
Never index beyond len - 1; append may reallocate, so always keep its return value.
Maps: m := map[string]int{"dosa": 60}; read with v, ok := m["idli"] to detect missing keys.
Structs: type Student struct { Name string; Marks int }; access fields with s.Name.
range walks slices (index, value) and maps (key, value); use _ to skip what you do not need.
Maps are unordered and not goroutine-safe; slices share backing arrays on copy.

interview.question: Slice vs array in Go?
interview.answer: Arrays have fixed length in the type ([3]int); slices ([]int) are growable views with pointer, len, cap. Nearly all code uses slices.

interview.question: What does append really do?
interview.answer: Adds to the slice, reallocating (usually doubling) when cap runs out. Always use the return: s = append(s, x) - the old header may point at stale memory.

interview.question: Comma-ok idiom - why?
interview.answer: v, ok := m[k] separates missing keys (zero value, false) from stored zero values (0, true). Without ok the two cases are indistinguishable.

interview.question: Why is map iteration random?
interview.answer: Go deliberately shuffles map order to stop programs depending on it. Need sorted output? Collect keys, sort them, then read.

topics.title: Functions, methods & errors
topics.definition: Functions package logic: func add(a, b int) int takes typed params and returns a typed result. Go functions can return multiple values, and errors are returned as values (not thrown) so callers handle them explicitly.
topics.analogy: Like a railway refund counter: you hand the form (arguments), the clerk either hands cash (result) or a rejection slip (error) - both come back across the same counter, and you must deal with whichever arrives.
keyPoints: Signature: func add(a int, b int) int - types after names, return type at the end.
Multiple returns: func div(a, b float64) (float64, error) - result plus error together.
Errors are values: if err != nil { ... } right after the call - handle, do not ignore.
Methods attach to structs: func (s Student) Passed() bool - receiver before the name.
defer runs at function exit (cleanup); named returns pair well with naked return.
Variadic: func sum(nums ...int) takes any count; pass a slice with sum(s...).

interview.question: Why does Go return errors instead of throwing?
interview.answer: Explicit handling: every failure path is visible at the call site, no hidden control flow. Forces developers to decide: handle, wrap (%w), or propagate.

interview.question: Method vs function - what changes?
interview.answer: Only the receiver: func (s T) M() binds behaviour to type T, enabling interfaces. Value receivers copy; pointer receivers (*T) mutate and avoid copies.

interview.question: What does defer do, and when does it run?
interview.answer: Defers a call until the surrounding function returns (LIFO order). Classic for closing files, unlocking mutexes - guaranteed cleanup even on error returns.

interview.question: When do multiple returns beat structs?
interview.answer: For result+error pairs and small tuples. Beyond 2-3 values, a named struct documents fields better than an anonymous tuple.

topics.title: Concurrency: goroutines & channels
topics.definition: Concurrency runs tasks together: go f() starts a lightweight goroutine; channels (chan) pass data safely between them. Buffered channels queue items; select waits on whichever message arrives first.
topics.analogy: Like a busy dosa counter: each cook (goroutine) works their own tawa, and the steel trays sliding between counter and tables (channels) carry plates safely - nobody grabs food from another cook’s hands.
keyPoints: go cook(order) starts a goroutine: cheap (KBs), thousands can run, scheduled by the Go runtime.
ch := make(chan int) creates a channel; ch <- 5 sends, x := <-ch receives (blocks till ready).
Unbuffered channels sync sender and receiver; make(chan int, 10) buffers ten without blocking.
sync.WaitGroup waits for a batch: Add(1) before each go, Done() inside, Wait() at the end.
select picks whichever channel is ready first - the heart of timeouts and fan-in merges.
Never copy a sync.Mutex; share by pointer or the lock silently stops working.

interview.question: Goroutine vs OS thread - why cheaper?
interview.answer: KB-sized stacks grown by the runtime, multiplexed M:N onto threads. Spawning thousands is normal; thousands of OS threads would exhaust memory.

interview.question: Unbuffered vs buffered channels?
interview.answer: Unbuffered: rendezvous, both sides sync each handoff. Buffered: queue up to cap without blocking. Unbuffered for sync points, buffered for smoothing bursts.

interview.question: What is select really doing?
interview.answer: Blocks until one branch can proceed, picks randomly among ready ones, runs default if given and none ready. Timeouts, cancellation and fan-in all build on it.

interview.question: When is a mutex better than a channel?
interview.answer: Channels move OWNERSHIP of data; mutexes guard SHARED state (counters, caches). Simple counter plus mutex beats channel ping-pong; pipelines prefer channels.

topics.title: Interfaces, embedding & composition
topics.definition: Methods are functions attached to a type via a receiver (func (r Rect) Area() float64). An interface is a set of method signatures; any type implementing them satisfies it implicitly (no 'implements' keyword). Go favours composition (embedding) over deep inheritance.
topics.analogy: Like a food-delivery app contract: an interface is the promise 'anything that can Deliver() and Track() is a Courier'. Zomato, Swiggy, Dunzo each satisfy it differently (value or pointer receivers) without ever declaring 'implements Courier'. Composition is adding a 'Driver' struct inside a 'Courier' to reuse fields.
keyPoints: Value receiver (r Rect) copies; pointer receiver (r *Rect) can mutate - be consistent within a type.
Interfaces are satisfied implicitly: define Area() float64 and your type is a Shape.
The empty interface any accepts anything - use sparingly; typed interfaces catch bugs at compile time.
Type assertions (s.(Rect)) and the comma-ok form (s.(Rect), ok) safely extract concrete types.
A type switch (switch v := x.(type)) branches on the dynamic type of an interface value.
Composition: embed struct B in A to reuse B's fields/methods - Go's answer to inheritance.

interview.question: Type assertion vs type switch?

topics.title: Concurrency patterns: WaitGroup, select & context
topics.definition: Go runs functions concurrently with the lightweight keyword go, and they communicate through typed channels instead of shared memory. sync.WaitGroup waits for a set of goroutines, buffered channels cap work in flight, and select picks whichever channel is ready first.
topics.analogy: Like an Indian dhaba kitchen: each go cook is a separate tawa (goroutine), the order tickets pinned to the wall are the channels, and the manager standing at the pass is select deciding which dish to plate next. The WaitGroup is the manager waiting until every tawa has finished its order.
keyPoints: go doWork() starts doWork immediately and does not wait - scheduling is done by the Go runtime, not by you.
A channel is a pipe: ch <- v sends, v := <-ch receives; unbuffered channels hand over the value only when both sides meet.
close(ch) signals no more values, which ends a for range ch loop cleanly.
A goroutine that sends to a channel nobody reads blocks forever and leaks - always pair sends with a receiver or a timeout.
Buffered channels (make(chan int, 10)) hold up to 10 values before the sender blocks, smoothing bursts of work.
select with a <-time.After(d) case adds a deadline to any wait, and a default case makes a receive non-blocking.

practice.hint: It blocks forever holding its stack and any captured memory.

interview.question: Goroutine vs OS thread - why is concurrency cheap in Go?
interview.answer: Goroutines start at a few KB of stack (grown on demand) and are multiplexed onto a small set of OS threads by the runtime scheduler. Spawning 1,000,000 goroutines is normal; 1,000,000 OS threads is not.

interview.question: Buffered vs unbuffered channel - when to pick each?
interview.answer: Unbuffered gives a strict rendezvous: the sender blocks until the receiver takes the value, which guarantees synchronisation. Buffered decouples producer and consumer up to the limit - good for bursts and queues, but it can hide back-pressure and delays.

interview.question: What is a select statement actually good for?
interview.answer: Waiting on multiple channels at once: timeouts (time.After), cancellation (done channels), and taking whichever result arrives first. A default branch turns the whole thing non-blocking.

interview.question: How do you avoid a data race without channels?
interview.answer: Guard shared state with sync.Mutex (or sync/atomic for counters), keeping the critical section tiny. But the idiomatic Go answer is still: share memory by communicating - pass ownership through a channel instead.

topics.title: HTTP services, JSON & data access
topics.definition: The net/http package builds servers and clients using only the standard library: ServeMux routes URL paths, handlers write status codes and bytes, and encoding/json maps Go structs to JSON through struct tags.
topics.analogy: Like a railway enquiry counter: the mux is the signboard telling each queue (route) which window to approach; the handler is the clerk who checks the ticket (request) and writes the reply; struct tags are the pre-printed form fields so customer details land in the right boxes.
keyPoints: mux.HandleFunc("/health", h) registers a route; a trailing slash makes the pattern match a whole subtree.
An http.HandlerFunc takes (w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) and is itself a type - pass it straight to HandleFunc.
Return JSON with w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") before w.WriteHeader(status).
Struct tags control the wire format: json:"user_name" renames, json:"-" hides a field entirely.
Only exported (capitalised) fields are marshalled - lowercase fields are silently ignored.
Decode with json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&payload) so malformed bodies surface as an error you can return.

interview.question: How does encoding/json decide what to marshal?
interview.answer: Only exported fields are considered and unexported ones are ignored silently. Names default to the Go field name unless a json tag renames them, and json:"-" excludes a field entirely.

interview.question: Explain http.ResponseWriter ordering rules.
interview.answer: Headers must be set before WriteHeader, and WriteHeader before writing the body. Writing implies 200 if WriteHeader was never called, and a second WriteHeader is ignored with a superfluous-write warning.

interview.question: ServeMux patterns: /health vs /item/ vs /?
interview.answer: Without a trailing slash a pattern matches only that exact path; with one it matches the whole subtree; / catches everything not matched more specifically. Go 1.22+ adds method and wildcard segments.

interview.question: How do you test an HTTP handler in Go?
interview.answer: Build a request with httptest.NewRequest, capture the result with httptest.NewRecorder, call the handler directly, then assert on rec.Code, rec.Header and rec.Body - no port or network involved.

topics.title: Testing, benchmarking & module hygiene
topics.definition: Go ships testing and benchmarking in the standard toolchain: _test.go files hold Test* functions using t.Error/t.Fatal, table-driven cases cover many inputs from one body, benchmarks measure with b.N, and go vet plus gofmt keep modules honest.
topics.analogy: Like a school exam plus a sports day on the same ground: a test is the written paper checking right or wrong, a benchmark is the stopwatch timing how fast you ran, and go vet with gofmt is the invigilator checking uniform and discipline before anyone even starts.
keyPoints: Test functions live in _test.go and take *testing.T: func TestAdd(t *testing.T) { ... }.
t.Errorf reports a failure and continues; t.Fatalf stops the test immediately - use Fatal when continuing would panic.
Table-driven tests put name/input/want in a slice and loop with t.Run(name, ...) for per-case reporting.
Benchmarks take *testing.B and loop for b.N iterations; run them with go test -bench=.
go vet catches suspicious constructs (wrong Printf verbs, unreachable code) that compile fine but are usually wrong.
gofmt -w . and go test ./... before every commit - the toolchain is the code review baseline.

interview.question: Why is table-driven testing the Go default?

interview.question: What does b.N mean in a benchmark?

interview.question: Why run go vet and -race in CI?

topics.title: Cloud-native patterns & production projects
topics.definition: Production Go services combine small deployable binaries, dependency injection through interfaces, structured logging, graceful shutdown via signals and context cancellation, and configuration from the environment. These habits are what take a program from a tutorial to a service you can run.
topics.analogy: Like running a highway dhaba during a bandh: the menu is fixed and posted (config from env), every order gets a numbered slip with a timer (context timeout), the manager can close the shutters politely while clearing the last tables (graceful shutdown), and the day's takings are written in a standard register (structured logs).
keyPoints: Contexts carry deadlines and cancellation: always accept ctx as the first parameter of anything that blocks or does I/O.
Depend on narrow interfaces, not concrete types - that is what makes code testable without a real database.
Read configuration from environment variables; keep secrets out of source and out of images.
log/slog gives structured, leveled logging that log aggregators can actually query.
Graceful shutdown: listen for SIGINT/SIGTERM, then stop accepting work and wait for in-flight requests to finish.
Ship a /health and a /ready endpoint, and make the binary statically built (CGO_ENABLED=0) for tiny container images.

practice.question: Why is `defer cancel()` mandatory after WithTimeout?
practice.hint: Think about the timer resource when cancel is skipped.
practice.answer: Without cancel the context timer is kept until it fires, so a tight loop leaks timers and memory. The Go vet lostcancel check flags exactly this. Cancelling early tells the runtime the resources are free.

interview.question: Why does Go pass context.Context first?
interview.answer: It is a convention the whole ecosystem relies on: cancellation and deadlines then propagate uniformly through servers, clients and databases. Putting it in a struct hides the lifetime and breaks tooling expectations.

interview.question: How does graceful shutdown protect users?
interview.answer: On SIGTERM the server stops accepting new connections, finishes in-flight requests within a deadline, flushes logs and closes database pools. Orchestrators send SIGTERM before SIGKILL, so finishing cleanly avoids dropped payments and half-written rows.

interview.question: Interfaces and dependency injection in Go - why does it fit?
interview.answer: Accepting a small interface instead of a concrete struct decouples business logic from infrastructure. Tests pass a fake with the same method set, no mocking framework needed, and production swaps in the real implementation.

interview.question: What makes a Go service cloud-native?
interview.answer: A single static binary, config from the environment, structured logs to stdout, health and readiness endpoints, context-aware shutdown, and no assumption about the local filesystem. Together those let the same image run anywhere.

topics.title: Toolchain, Cargo & first program
topics.definition: Rust is a compiled, statically-typed systems language guaranteeing memory safety without a garbage collector. You manage projects with Cargo (build tool + package manager); rustc compiles, the borrow checker verifies safety.
topics.analogy: Like a bank locker with two keys: you (the owner) can lend items, but the guard (borrow checker) ensures only one person mutates at a time and nothing is taken twice — safety checked before the vault opens.
keyPoints: Install via rustup (rustup.rs); verify with `rustc --version` and `cargo --version`.
Create a project: `cargo new hello`; run it: `cargo run`; release build: `cargo run --release`.
Entry point is `fn main()` in src/main.rs; print with `println!` (a macro — note the !).
Variables are immutable by default: `let x = 5;` cannot change; add `mut` to allow it.
Types are inferred but fixed: `let city = "Bengaluru";` locks city to &str.
Compiler errors are lessons, not insults — read them top-down; they often suggest the fix.

interview.question: immutable by default — why?
