topics.title: Variables, types & control flow
topics.definition: Rust variables are immutable and typed (inferred but fixed): integers (i32), floats (f64), bool, char. Control flow uses if/else (expressions returning values), loop, while, for, and match for exhaustive branching.
topics.analogy: Like ink vs pencil in a school notebook: let writes in permanent ink (immutable); let mut is pencil (erasable). if/else is the teacher choosing remarks by marks; match is the report card covering EVERY grade — no student left ungraded.
keyPoints: Scalar types: i32/u32, f64, bool, char (Unicode!); annotate once (let x: i32 = 5) or let inference decide.
Shadowing (let x = x + 1) re-declares with a new value/type — different from mut reassignment.
if is an expression: let g = if m >= 90 {"A"} else {"B"}; — no ternary operator needed.
loop runs forever until break (which can return a value); while and for cover the rest.
match must be exhaustive: every possible value needs an arm, or _ catches the rest.
Integer division truncates (7 / 2 == 3); compare floats with care, not ==.

interview.question: mut vs shadowing — difference?
interview.answer: mut reassigns the SAME binding (type fixed). Shadowing declares a NEW binding that may even change type. Use mut for updates, shadowing for transformations.

interview.question: Why is match exhaustive, and what is _?
interview.answer: The compiler forces every possible value to be handled — missing cases fail compilation. _ is the wildcard catching the rest, guaranteeing coverage.

interview.question: if is an expression — what does that imply?
interview.answer: Branches return values, so let g = if c {a} else {b} works. Both arms must yield the same type; it replaces the ternary operator entirely.

interview.question: .. vs ..= in ranges?
interview.answer: 1..5 excludes 5 (1-4); 1..=5 includes it (1-5). Off-by-one bugs hide here — read the = as "equals included".

topics.title: Ownership & borrowing
topics.definition: Ownership is Rusts memory system with no garbage collector: each value has exactly one owner, moves transfer ownership, borrows (& references) let code look without taking, and values die when their owner leaves scope.
topics.analogy: Like a library book: one current holder (owner), lending to a friend moves it (move), letting someone read over your shoulder is a borrow (&), and returning it to the shelf (drop) ends it. The librarian (borrow checker) never allows two writers at once.
keyPoints: Each value has ONE owner; assigning (let b = a) MOVES Strings - a is unusable after.
Copy types (i32, bool, char) duplicate cheaply instead of moving; Clone makes explicit deep copies.
Immutable borrows (&x) allow many readers; mutable borrows (&mut x) allow exactly one writer, never both together.
References must never outlive their data - the compiler rejects dangling pointers at build time.
Functions take ownership (fn eat(s: String)) or borrow (fn read(s: &String)) - pick by intent.
Slices (&s[0..5]) borrow part of a collection without copying - string processing lives on slices.

interview.question: What is ownership in one breath?
interview.answer: Each value has one owner; moves transfer it; borrows allow temporary access; values drop when owners leave scope - memory safety without a garbage collector.

interview.question: Move vs Copy vs Clone?
interview.answer: Move: ownership transfers (heap types). Copy: implicit bitwise duplicate (small stack types). Clone: explicit deep copy (may allocate). Interviews love which types are Copy.

interview.question: Borrow checker rules?
interview.answer: Unlimited immutable borrows OR exactly one mutable borrow, never mixed while alive; references must not outlive data. Violations are compile errors, not runtime bugs.

interview.question: Why no garbage collector - benefit?
interview.answer: Zero runtime pause, no background thread, predictable performance for systems code; the cost is learning to satisfy the checker upfront.

topics.title: Structs, enums & match
topics.definition: Structs bundle named fields into one type. Enums list possible shapes, often carrying data. Match handles every case and can pull the carried values out while checking.
topics.analogy: Like a railway reservation form: a struct is the filled passenger record with name, age, and berth. An enum is the ticket-status stamp, either Confirmed with a seat number or Waiting with a queue number, and match is the examiner reading each stamp correctly.
keyPoints: Define with struct Student { name: String, marks: u32 } and build with Student { name: ..., marks: ... }.
Update with ..old syntax and construct with helper functions such as Student::new.
Enums carry data: enum Ticket { Confirmed(u32), Waiting(u32) } holds different payloads.
Match must cover all cases: each arm can bind payloads like Confirmed(seat).
Use methods with impl blocks: fn passed(&self) reads without taking ownership.
Derive Debug for printing and Clone when copies are needed.

interview.question: Struct versus enum?
interview.answer: A struct combines several fields that occur together. An enum chooses one shape from several alternatives, each optionally carrying different data.

interview.question: What does exhaustive match guarantee?
interview.answer: Every possible value has handling code, so new variants break compilation until handled. This prevents silent unhandled cases.

interview.question: When should methods take &self?
interview.answer: When they only read the object. Use &mut self for mutation and self when intentionally consuming the value.

interview.question: Why is Option better than null?
interview.answer: Option makes absence visible in the type, so the compiler forces Some and None handling. Null hides absence and causes runtime crashes.

topics.title: Collections: Vec, String & HashMap
topics.definition: Vec<T> is a growable typed array; String is growable UTF-8 text (vs borrowed &str); HashMap<K,V> maps keys to values. All are heap-allocated, owned values that move, borrow and drop like everything else.
topics.analogy: Like a wedding guest list: Vec is the extendable register (push more names as RSVPs arrive); String is the erasable whiteboard (push_str edits freely) vs the printed card (&str); HashMap is the seating chart mapping table numbers to family names.
keyPoints: Vec: let mut v = vec![1, 2]; v.push(3); v[0]; v.len(); v.iter() borrows each item.
Indexing v[i] panics if out of bounds; v.get(i) returns Option for safe access.
String vs &str: String owns and grows (push_str); &str borrows a view; "lit" is &str, to_string() converts.
Iterate strings by .chars() (Unicode-safe) not bytes; never index a String with [i].
HashMap: map.insert(k, v); map.get(&k) gives Option<&V>; entry(k).or_insert(0) counts in one pass.
Ownership applies: passing a Vec moves it unless borrowed (&v) or cloned (v.clone()).

topics.title: Errors: Result, Option & unwrap habits
topics.definition: Rust has no exceptions: functions return Result<T, E> (success or failure) and Option<T> (value or nothing). match, ?, unwrap and combinators handle them - the compiler forces every failure path to be addressed.
topics.analogy: Like a parcel counter with two slips: Result is delivered-or-returned (you MUST sign for either), Option is full-or-empty locker (you check before reaching in). ? is handing the return slip straight up the chain instead of queuing twice.

match handles every arm explicitly; if let handles one case and ignores the rest.

unwrap() panics on failure: fine in examples, banned in production and interviews.
ok_or turns Option into Result with a chosen error; ok() turns Result into Option.
Combinators map, and_then, unwrap_or chain without nesting: opt.map(|v| v + 1).unwrap_or(0).

topics.title: Traits & generics
topics.definition: Traits define shared behavior (methods a type must provide) like interfaces. Generics write code once that works for many types. Together they give reusable, type-safe abstractions with zero runtime cost.
topics.analogy: Like a Swiggy delivery contract: a trait says "anyone delivering must have ride() and deliver(). A bike rider and a cyclist both sign it (implement the trait). Generics is one delivery app that works for any vehicle without rewriting code for each.
keyPoints: Define a trait: trait Speak { fn speak(&self) -> String; } and implement it per type with impl Speak for Dog { ... }.
impl Trait for Type must implement EVERY required method or the compiler errors.
Generics: fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T works for any comparable type.
Trait bounds (T: Trait) restrict generics to types that implement the trait.
Derive traits for free: #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] prints, clones and compares structs.
The blanket impl pattern lets the stdlib auto-implement traits (like ToString) for your types.

interview.question: Traits vs interfaces (Java) — similarities and differences?
interview.answer: Both define shared behavior. Rust traits support default methods, associated types, and can be implemented for types you do not own (e.g. your trait on Vec), unlike Java interfaces on your own classes only.

interview.question: What is monomorphization and why does Rust generics cost nothing at runtime?
interview.answer: The compiler generates a concrete function/struct per used type at compile time. No boxing, no vtables for generics — as fast as hand-written code, at the cost of larger binaries.

interview.question: Static dispatch vs dynamic dispatch (impl Trait vs &dyn Trait)?
interview.answer: impl Trait / <T: Trait> is static: known type, monomorphized, fastest. &dyn Trait is dynamic: one call site, vtable lookup, allows heterogeneous collections. Pick static by default.

interview.question: What is the orphan rule?
interview.answer: You can implement a trait for a type only if the trait OR the type is local to your crate. Prevents conflicting impls across crates; worked around with newtype wrappers.

topics.title: Iterators & closures
topics.definition: Iterators produce a sequence of values lazily; closures are anonymous functions that can capture their environment. Chained adapters (map, filter, fold) express data transforms clearly and usually compile to the same speed as hand-written loops.
topics.analogy: Like a juice counter workflow: the fruit basket is the collection, the peeler/filter/strainer are iterator adapters, and a closure is a one-line recipe card ("peel only ripe mangoes"). Nothing runs until you actually pour the glass (collect).
keyPoints: Calling .iter()/iter_mut()/into_iter() borrows or takes elements; loops over them lazily.
Adapters (map, filter, take, skip) are lazy — they do nothing until a consumer runs.
Consumers (collect, sum, count, for_each) drive the pipeline and produce the result.
Closures: |x| x + 1; use move to take ownership of captured variables.
fold is the general accumulator (reduce): list.iter().fold(0, |acc, x| acc + x).
IteRators avoid intermediate allocations and often beat index loops in benchmarks.

topics.title: Concurrency: threads, channels & async
topics.definition: Fearless concurrency means the compiler checks thread safety. std::thread::spawn runs closures on new threads, channels (mpsc) pass values between them, Arc<Mutex<T>> shares mutable state safely, and async/await handles thousands of waiting tasks on few threads.
topics.analogy: Like a railway station with parallel platforms: threads are separate trains running at the same time. A channel is the parcel trolley that safely hands bags from one train to the next. Arc<Mutex<T>> is a single ticket window with one counter clerk and a queue outside. async is one booking clerk handling a thousand phone calls by putting each on hold instead of waiting.
keyPoints: thread::spawn(|| ...) starts a thread; join() waits for it and returns its Result.
mpsc::channel() gives a sender and receiver - many senders, one receiver, values move across.
Arc<T> shares ownership across threads; Mutex<T> allows one thread inside the lock at a time.
Never share &mut across threads: the borrow checker rejects it at compile time, not at 2 AM.
Send marks types safe to move to another thread; Sync marks them safe to share by reference.
async fn with .await yields instead of blocking - ideal for I/O-heavy servers; use a runtime like tokio.

interview.question: How does Rust prevent data races at compile time?
interview.answer: Ownership plus Send/Sync: the borrow checker rejects aliased mutation and moving non-Send values across threads before the program ever runs.

interview.question: Arc vs Rc?
interview.answer: Rc is fast but single-threaded (non-atomic); Arc uses atomic reference counting and is Send/Sync, so it is the only choice across threads.

interview.question: Mutex vs RwLock - pick one and defend it.
interview.answer: Mutex: simpler, best when writes are common. RwLock: many concurrent readers with rare writes (caches, config), higher read throughput.

interview.question: What does .await actually do?
interview.answer: It yields control back to the runtime so other tasks progress while this one waits, then resumes where it left off. Without .await the future does nothing.

topics.title: Smart pointers, lifetimes & interior mutability
topics.definition: Smart pointers are structs that act like pointers but add behaviour: Box<T> moves data to the heap, Rc<T> shares ownership by reference counting, RefCell<T> permits mutation through a shared reference. Lifetimes (a) tell the compiler how long references stay valid so it can guarantee no dangling pointer.
topics.analogy: Like a public library: Box is a book issued to exactly one reader (single owner on the heap). Rc is a reference book with a counter card - every reader ticks it and it returns to the shelf only when the last tick is crossed out. RefCell is the notebook anyone may read but only the librarian writes in, with the rule checked at the door rather than at printing time. Lifetimes are the due-date stamp proving you still hold the book legally.
keyPoints: Box<T> = single heap owner; also required for recursive types like linked lists and trait objects.
Rc<T> counts owners; the value drops when the count hits zero. Single-threaded only - use Arc across threads.
RefCell<T> moves borrow checking to runtime: it panics instead of failing to compile. That is the trade.
Lifetime annotations never change how long a value lives - they describe an existing relationship to the compiler.
Most lifetimes are elided; annotate when several references make the rule ambiguous (structs, multi-ref fns).
static is the longest lifetime: string literals are &static str, valid for the whole program.

interview.question: Box vs Rc vs RefCell - one line each?
interview.answer: Box: single heap owner, zero overhead. Rc: shared single-threaded ownership with a count. RefCell: mutation through shared refs, checked at runtime.

interview.question: What is interior mutability and when do you accept it?
interview.answer: Mutation while appearing immutable, e.g. RefCell or Mutex. Accept it when sharing must go through a shared reference and the runtime check is a fair trade.

interview.question: Do lifetime annotations extend a value life?
interview.answer: No. They only describe a relationship the compiler already enforces. They can never make a dangling reference valid.

interview.question: Why does a recursive enum need Box?
interview.answer: A type containing itself directly has infinite size, so the compiler cannot allocate it. Box adds one pointer level, fixing the size while keeping the recursion.

topics.title: Advanced: iterators, closures & production mindset
topics.definition: Iterators are lazy, chainable pipelines (map, filter, fold) that do no work until consumed. Closures capture their environment. Combined with Rust tooling (clippy, fmt, doc tests), they are how real Rust code is written.
topics.analogy: Like a food processing line in a modern factory: raw mangoes come in, a washer (map), a ripeness checker (filter) and a packing machine (fold) sit along the belt, and nothing moves until a customer order (consume) starts the line. Closures are the workers who remember the recipe board of their section.
keyPoints: Iterators are lazy: nothing runs until a consumer like collect(), sum() or for_each() pulls items.
map transforms, filter keeps matches, take/skip bound the count, and they chain without intermediate vectors.
collect() needs a type hint when ambiguous: let v: Vec<i32> = iter.collect();
fold(init, |acc, x| ...) reduces to one value; sum() and count() are shortcuts.
Closures capture by reference by default; move forces ownership transfer into the closure.
Use clippy for lint advice, rustfmt for formatting, and /// doc comments for doc tests.

interview.question: Why are Rust iterators zero-cost?
interview.answer: Laziness plus monomorphisation lets the compiler fuse a chain into a single loop with no heap allocation, matching hand-written indexing speed.

interview.question: iter() vs iter_mut() vs into_iter()?
interview.answer: iter borrows items; iter_mut borrows them mutably; into_iter consumes the collection and yields owned values. Pick by whether you need to keep or mutate the source.

interview.question: How do closures capture, and what does move change?
interview.answer: By reference by default (least privilege that works: &, &mut, then by value). move forces capture by value, required when the closure must outlive the scope, e.g. threads.

interview.question: filter_map vs filter().map()?
interview.answer: filter_map combines both in one pass and lets each step return None to drop an item - fewer passes and no Option plumbing compared to chaining.

topics.title: .NET setup & your first program
topics.definition: C# (C-sharp) is a statically-typed, object-oriented language running on .NET. You write .cs files; the compiler builds them to IL (Intermediate Language) and the .NET runtime (CLR) executes it with garbage collection.
topics.analogy: Like ordering via a standard railway catering contract: you write the order (C#), the kitchen translator (compiler) converts it to a universal slip (IL), and every pantry car (.NET runtime) fulfils it identically.
keyPoints: Install the .NET SDK; verify with `dotnet --version`; scaffold with `dotnet new console -n Hello`.
Run with `dotnet run` inside the project folder; entry point is top-level statements or `static void Main()`.
Statically typed: `string name = "Asha"; int marks = 92;` — mismatches fail at compile time.
`Console.WriteLine()` prints; `Console.ReadLine()` reads text (nullable string — handle null!).
Statements end with semicolons; { } braces define blocks; file-scoped namespaces keep code tidy.
Top-level statements (no Main boilerplate) are the modern default for small programs.

interview.question: C# + .NET: how does code actually run?
interview.answer: C# compiles to IL assemblies; the CLR JIT-compiles IL to machine code at runtime, with garbage collection, type safety and exception handling.

interview.question: What are top-level statements?
interview.answer: C# 9+ sugar letting small programs skip Program/Main boilerplate — the compiler generates the entry point for you.

interview.question: Why is Console.ReadLine() typed string? (nullable)?
interview.answer: It can return null (e.g. redirected input ends), so the nullable annotation forces you to handle that case.

interview.question: Value types vs reference types — quick version?
interview.answer: Value types (int, struct) hold data directly and copy on assignment; reference types (string, class) hold a reference to heap data. Affects nullability, copying and performance.

topics.title: Types, variables & operators
topics.definition: C# variables have fixed static types: value types (int, double, bool, char, decimal) hold data directly; string holds text. Operators (+, -, *, /, %, ==, &&, ||, !) compute and compare; var infers the type but never loosens it.
topics.analogy: Like reserved train berths: an int berth fits exactly one whole-number passenger; var is the TTE reading your ticket and writing the coach name for you — the berth stays fixed, only the paperwork is automatic.
keyPoints: Value types: int, long, double, decimal (money!), bool, char; reference default string for text.
var city = "X" infers string but stays string — city = 5 afterwards fails compilation.
Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 is 3; 7.0 / 2 is 3.5; 7 % 2 is the remainder 1.
Use decimal (99.50m) for money, double for science — floats cannot represent 0.1 exactly.
== compares values for primitives and strings (string overloads it); objects compare references unless overridden.
Convert with int.Parse / double.Parse (throw on bad input) or TryParse (returns bool, no exception).

interview.question: var: dynamic typing or not? Explain.
interview.answer: Fully static: var only skips WRITING the type; the compiler infers and locks it. x = "hi" then x = 5 fails. True dynamic behaviour needs the dynamic keyword.

interview.question: double vs decimal — which for money?
interview.answer: decimal (base-10 exact, 28 digits) for money; double (binary, fast) for science/graphics. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in double — unacceptable in billing.

interview.question: Parse vs TryParse vs Convert?
interview.answer: Parse: throws FormatException on bad input. TryParse: returns false, no throw — best for user input. Convert: null-tolerant (null -> 0). Never Parse raw user input.

interview.question: Value type vs reference type — quick version?
interview.answer: Value types (int, struct) store data inline and copy on assignment; reference types (string, class) store a heap address and share. Affects nullability, copying cost and == behaviour.

topics.title: Conditions, loops & arrays
topics.definition: if/else and switch choose paths; for, while and foreach repeat work; arrays (int[]) store fixed-size sequences by index. Together they solve most beginner programs before collections arrive.
topics.analogy: Like a school assembly line: if it rains shift indoors else stay out (condition); the teacher repeats instructions row by row (loop); the class register is a fixed 60-slot array where slot 0 is the first student.
keyPoints: if / else if / else runs the first true branch; switch matches one value against case labels.
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) counts exactly; foreach (var x in arr) walks values directly.
while checks before each round; do-while runs once first - both need progress toward exit.
Arrays: int[] a = new int[5]; indexes 0..4; a.Length gives size; index 5 throws.
break exits the loop; continue skips to the next round; both pair with if.
Compare strings with == (overloaded for content) but watch nulls: use "Sun".Equals(day) style or string.Equals.

interview.question: for vs foreach vs while?
interview.answer: for: need index or mutation. foreach: read every value simply (read-only over the enumerator). while: unknown rounds like reading until EOF.

interview.question: What happens at marks[5] on 3 elements?
interview.answer: IndexOutOfRangeException at runtime. Arrays are fixed-size: check i < arr.Length, or use List<T> for growth.

interview.question: Why does switch need break?
interview.answer: Without it execution falls through into the next case. Stacked labels share intentionally; otherwise missing break is a bug - switch expressions (=>) avoid it.

interview.question: == on strings - safe?
interview.answer: Yes for content: string overloads == for value comparison (handles nulls safely too). For objects generally == means reference unless overloaded.

topics.title: Methods, parameters & overloading
topics.definition: Methods package behaviour inside classes. Parameters supply input, return supplies output, and overloads give the same name different parameter shapes. Optional parameters and out variables handle common variations.
topics.analogy: Like a canteen counter with one order window: regular meals, mini meals, and parcel orders all use the same window but different slips. Overloads are those slips, each complete in its own way.
keyPoints: Define with access, return, name, and parameters: static int Add(int a, int b).
Call with position or names: Add(4, 6) or Add(b: 6, a: 4).
Return exits immediately; every path in a non-void method must return a value.
Overloads differ by parameter count or types, not by return type alone.
Optional parameters need defaults and must come last: Fee(int age = 10).
Use out for extra results: TryGet(name, out marks) returns success plus value.

practice.question: Why must all paths return?

interview.question: Static versus instance methods?
interview.answer: Static belongs to the type and needs no object; instance works on object fields through this. Stateless helpers go static, stateful behaviour goes instance.

interview.question: How are overloads resolved?
interview.answer: By parameter count and types at compile time. Return type alone cannot distinguish them, and ambiguous calls fail compilation.

interview.question: Optional parameters versus overloads?
interview.answer: Optional parameters suit small defaults; overloads suit genuinely different shapes or behaviour. Too many optionals make calls hard to read.

interview.question: What does out do?
interview.answer: It lets a method return an extra value through a parameter. Callers declare the variable inline, and the method must assign it before returning.

topics.title: Collections, LINQ & generics
topics.definition: List<T> is the resizable typed array; Dictionary<K,V> maps keys to values; HashSet<T> holds uniques. LINQ (Where, Select, OrderBy, Sum) queries any collection declaratively; generics (List<T>, methods with <T>) reuse logic across types safely.
topics.analogy: Like a ration shop ledger: List<T> is the growing item register; Dictionary is the card-number-to-family map; HashSet is the unique-token bowl; LINQ is the clerk answering in plain words - all bills above 500, sorted, totalled - without you counting pages.
keyPoints: List<string> cart = new() { "idli", "dosa" }; cart.Add("vada"); cart[0]; cart.Count.
Dictionary<string,int> price = new() { ["idli"] = 30 }; TryGetValue avoids KeyNotFoundException.
HashSet<string> seen dedups and tests membership fast; handy for visitedIds.
LINQ: marks.Where(m => m >= 40).OrderBy(m => m).ToList(); Select transforms; Sum/Average aggregate.
Deferred execution: queries run when enumerated - ToList() snapshots results now.
Generics: T First<T>(List<T> xs) works for any type with full compile-time safety.

interview.question: List<T> vs array vs IEnumerable<T>?
interview.answer: array: fixed, fastest index. List<T>: resizable with methods. IEnumerable<T>: read-forward sequence (often lazy LINQ) - pick by growth and laziness needs.

interview.question: What is deferred execution?
interview.answer: LINQ builds the query now but runs it on enumeration, seeing latest data. Surprises stale readers and repeats work - ToList() when you need a snapshot.

interview.question: Dictionary lookup complexity?
interview.answer: Average O(1) via hashing; worst O(n) on pathological collisions. Needs correct GetHashCode/Equals on custom keys.

interview.question: Why generics over object lists?
interview.answer: Type safety at compile time, no casting, no boxing for value types - List<int> beats ArrayList on all three.

topics.title: OOP: classes, objects & properties
topics.definition: Classes blueprint objects: fields store data, properties guard access with get/set, constructors initialise, methods act. Objects (new Student()) carry their own state and behaviour.
topics.analogy: Like an Aadhaar enrolment form: the blank form (class) defines fields, each filled card (object) holds one person’s data, the officer window (property) checks values before stamping, and the queue token (constructor) starts every card correctly.
keyPoints: class Student { } blueprints; new Student() builds an object with its own field copies.
Constructors (public Student(name)) run at creation; chain with : this(...) for defaults.
Properties expose guarded access: public int Marks { get; private set; } reads freely, writes inside only.
Auto-properties { get; set; } for plain data; full properties with backing fields for validation.
static belongs to the class itself (Math.PI, counters); instance members belong to each object.
Records (record Student(name, marks)) give tiny immutable data types with equality built in.

interview.question: Field vs property vs auto-property?
interview.answer: Field: raw storage. Property: guarded gate with logic. Auto-property: shorthand when no logic is needed yet - upgrade later without breaking callers.

interview.question: Why validate inside the setter?
interview.answer: The object defends its own rules at the boundary, so no caller can sneak in bad data. Fail fast with exceptions, not silent corruption.

interview.question: static vs instance - memory picture?
interview.answer: Instance: one copy per object on the heap. static: one copy on the type itself for the app lifetime. Counters and factories live static; personal data lives instance.

interview.question: class vs record vs struct?
interview.answer: class: reference, mutable, identity equality. record: reference, value equality, with-copies. struct: value type, copied on assignment - small immutable values only.

topics.title: Inheritance & polymorphism
topics.definition: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend a base class: Derived : Base. Polymorphism lets a base reference hold derived objects, and virtual/override methods pick the derived behaviour at runtime.
topics.analogy: Like a family tiffin business passed to the next generation: the child inherits the recipe book (base fields/methods) and adds new dishes, but a customer who ordered the family "Special" gets the child’s improved version automatically - same order, upgraded plate.
keyPoints: Declare with : Base - a single base class plus any number of interfaces.
base(...) calls the parent constructor; base.Method() calls the parent method.
Mark base methods virtual and derived ones override to swap behaviour at runtime.
Every class ultimately derives from object, so ToString/Equals are always available.
Prefer composition over deep inheritance chains; more than 2 levels is a smell.
sealed stops further inheritance; protected exposes members to derived classes only.

practice.hint: new shadows; override replaces the slot.

interview.question: override vs new (method hiding)?
interview.answer: override replaces the base implementation for ALL references (virtual dispatch). new just hides it for the derived type only; a base reference still calls the base version - a classic foot-gun.

interview.question: Why favour composition over inheritance?
interview.answer: Deep hierarchies create fragile base-class problems - a base change ripples everywhere. Composed behaviour is swappable at runtime and far easier to test.

interview.question: What does every class inherit implicitly?
interview.answer: object, giving ToString/Equals/GetHashCode/GetType. Override ToString for readable output and Equals for value equality.

interview.question: Can you inherit from multiple classes?
interview.answer: No single implementation inheritance in C# - one class base only. Multiple interfaces can be implemented, which is how multiple-type behaviour is achieved.

topics.title: Interfaces, exceptions & files
topics.definition: Interfaces declare contracts (what) that classes implement (how). Exceptions signal failures through try/catch/finally, and using plus File/StreamReader handle files and clean resource release.
topics.analogy: Like a government form scheme: the interface is the blank printed form every office must fill (same fields), each department is a class filling it differently. try/catch is the enquiry counter catching rejected forms, and using is the staff auto-returning your file after processing.
keyPoints: interface IShape { double Area(); } - pure contract, no fields, all public by default.
A class can implement many interfaces - the C# answer to multiple inheritance.
try runs risky code, catch handles specific exceptions, finally always runs (cleanup).
Throw precise exceptions: ArgumentNullException, InvalidOperationException - not bare Exception.
using var f = ... disposes the resource automatically even on exceptions (IDisposable).
Let exceptions bubble with useful messages; catch only what you can genuinely handle.

practice.answer: // TryParse returns false with no stack unwind - use it for normal bad input, exceptions for truly exceptional states

interview.question: Interface vs abstract class?
interview.answer: Interface: pure contract, many can be implemented, no state/implementation (except default methods). Abstract class: shared code and fields, single inheritance. Use interfaces for capabilities, abstract classes for common base logic.

interview.question: When should you catch an exception?
interview.answer: Only when you can add value - retry, translate to a domain error, or log-and-continue. Swallowing (catch { }) hides bugs; let unknown exceptions bubble to a top-level handler.

interview.question: What does finally guarantee?
interview.answer: It runs on normal completion AND on exception - the guaranteed cleanup hook. Combined with using (which compiles to try/finally) resources never leak.

interview.question: Why does using beat manual Close?
interview.answer: It becomes try/finally under the hood, so Dispose runs even on exceptions or early return - impossible to forget on the error path.

topics.title: Async, await & Task
topics.definition: async/await writes asynchronous code that reads top-to-bottom. A Task represents work in progress; await yields control until it finishes, keeping the calling thread free. Task.WhenAll runs jobs in parallel.
topics.analogy: Like ordering five dishes at a restaurant: instead of staring at the kitchen for each dish (blocking), you place all orders, sit back, and get notified as each arrives (await). Task.WhenAll is calling the whole table together once every dish lands.
keyPoints: Mark methods async Task; use await on Tasks - the method resumes where it paused.
await never blocks the thread - it returns control, so UIs stay responsive.
Task.WhenAll(a, b) runs both concurrently and waits for all; Task.WhenAny waits for the first.
Async all the way up: do not mix blocking .Result / .Wait() with async (deadlock risk).
Use CancellationToken to cancel long tasks (timeouts, user cancel).
For CPU-bound work use Task.Run; for I/O-bound rely on naturally async APIs (HttpClient, streams).

practice.hint: Blocks the thread and can deadlock on a captured context.
practice.answer: // .Result/.Wait() block and can deadlock - always await instead

interview.question: What problem does async/await solve?
interview.answer: It keeps threads free during I/O waits so apps scale (thousands of concurrent requests) and stay responsive, while code still reads top-to-bottom instead of nested callbacks.

interview.question: async Task vs async void?
interview.answer: async Task is awaitable and propagates errors. async void is fire-and-forget, cannot be awaited, and throws crash the process - only for UI event handlers.

interview.question: Task.WhenAll vs sequential awaits?
interview.answer: WhenAll starts all tasks then waits - total time is the longest task. Sequential awaits run one after another - total is the sum. Wrong choice can 10x a page load.

interview.question: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound async?
interview.answer: I/O-bound: use naturally async APIs (await file/network). CPU-bound: Task.Run off the UI thread, since await alone does not speed up computation.

topics.title: Delegates, events & LINQ deep dive
topics.definition: Delegates are type-safe method pointers; Func/Action/Predicate are the built-in generic ones. Events let objects notify subscribers. LINQ (query and method syntax) filters, maps, and aggregates sequences declaratively.
topics.analogy: Like a newspaper subscription: the publisher (event) does not know who reads; you subscribe (event handler) and get each edition (callback). LINQ is the newsroom editor - Describe "give me headlines above 80", not the step-by-step sorting.
keyPoints: Func<T, TResult> returns a value; Action<T> returns void; Predicate<T> returns bool.
Lambdas are inline functions: x => x * x; multiple statements need braces and return.
LINQ method chains (Where/Select/OrderBy) are usually clearer than query syntax for filtering.
Where filters, Select maps, OrderBy sorts, GroupBy buckets, Aggregate reduces.
LINQ uses deferred execution - the query runs when you enumerate (foreach/ToList).
Events follow publisher + subscribe (+=) / unsubscribe (-=) for loose coupling.

practice.answer: // Runs at foreach/ToList/Count - not at declaration

interview.question: Deferred vs immediate LINQ execution?
interview.answer: Deferred (Where/Select): builds a query, runs on each enumeration, sees latest data. Immediate (ToList/Count/ToArray): runs once, snapshots. Confusing them causes phantom rows.

interview.question: Func vs Action vs Predicate?
interview.answer: Func<TResult> returns a value; Action returns void; Predicate<T> is Func<T,bool> for conditions. Choose by whether the lambda produces a result.

interview.question: Why use events over direct method calls?
interview.answer: Events decouple publisher from subscriber: the publisher raises, any number of listeners react, added/removed at runtime - the observer pattern that keeps UI and logic independent.

interview.question: Where does LINQ fall short?
interview.answer: Complex multi-stage pipelines can hurt performance and debuggability; hot loops may need plain foreach. Also a database provider must translate it to SQL - unsupported methods throw at runtime.

topics.title: File I/O, error handling & LINQ
topics.definition: try/catch/finally handle exceptions; using disposes resources deterministically. LINQ composes queries (Where, Select, GroupBy, Aggregate) over any IEnumerable with deferred execution and method-chain syntax.
topics.analogy: Like a dabbawala sorting office: try is sorting tiffins, catch handles a broken latch (exception) without stopping the whole route, finally closes the shop (cleanup) either way, and LINQ is the routing table that filters, groups and totals dabbas in one readable pipeline.
keyPoints: try risky code; catch (specific) handles known failures; finally always runs (cleanup).
throw; re-throws preserving the stack; throw ex; resets it - prefer the bare throw in catch.
using var f = ... guarantees Dispose even on exception; preferred over manual finally.
LINQ method chains: list.Where(...).Select(...).OrderBy(...); query syntax reads like SQL.
Deferred execution: the query runs only when enumerated (foreach/ToList), not when built.
Aggregate folds a list into one value; GroupBy buckets; SelectMany flattens nested collections.

practice.question: Read a file line by line and count non-empty lines.
Why is `throw ex;` discouraged in a catch block?
practice.answer: Use bare `throw;` to preserve the original stack. `throw ex;` marks the catch line as the new origin, hiding where the error truly began.

interview.question: Deferred vs immediate LINQ execution?
interview.answer: Most operators are lazy: the query is a blueprint, executed on enumeration (foreach/ToList/ToArray). Aggregators (Count, Sum, ToList) force immediate execution. Adding to the source after building but before enumerating changes results.

interview.question: Where vs First vs Single?
interview.answer: Where returns a lazy filtered stream (0..n). First returns the first or throws; FirstOrDefault returns default instead. Single throws unless EXACTLY one matches - use for uniqueness guarantees.

interview.question: finally vs a finalizer (destructor)?
interview.answer: finally runs deterministically when a try block exits; a finalizer runs at GC time, non-deterministically, and is slow. Use finally/using for cleanup, never rely on destructors.

interview.question: Why prefer exception filters (catch when)?
interview.answer: catch (HttpException e) when (e.Status == 404) logs/handles only that case without unwinding and re-catching, keeping related handling in one place and preserving the stack.

intro: This topic, "File I/O, error handling & LINQ", is your step into a bigger idea, and it builds directly on everything you have learned so far. We will start from the very beginning: what this concept actually means, why it exists, and how it is used in everyday programs — never assuming you already know the jargon.

At its core, try/catch/finally handle exceptions; using disposes resources deterministically. linq composes queries (where, select, groupby, aggregate) over any ienumerable with deferred execution and method-chain syntax.. If you are not sure of a word we use, pause and check it: each one is defined in plain language in the key points that follow.

Think about it through a real-world analogy before touching code: Like a dabbawala sorting office: try is sorting tiffins, catch handles a broken latch (exception) without stopping the whole route, finally closes the shop (cleanup) either way, and LINQ is the routing table that filters, groups and totals dabbas in one readable pipeline.. This mental picture is the fastest way to remember the shape of the idea when you meet it again in a real project.

The key points below are the minimum you need. Notice how each one connects to the last — that is how knowledge sticks. After each point you will see a tiny example you can run, followed by one that slowly grows in difficulty, so you can watch the idea work from start to finish.
Never stop at reading the examples. Type them into your editor, change a value, break it on purpose, and read the error. That loop — write, run, break, fix — is where the concept becomes yours.

Finally, test yourself with the practice questions and the interview questions. The interview questions are the "why" behind the "how": they are the ones that reappear in real work and in technical interviews, and we have written them to be answerable from the explanations above.

topics.title: Building apps: APIs, testing & best practices
topics.definition: Modern C# apps combine layered architecture (controllers, services, repositories), dependency injection, REST APIs, and xUnit testing. Best practices - nullable reference types, records, and clean boundaries - keep large codebases maintainable.
topics.analogy: Like running a well-organised restaurant: the waiter (controller/API) takes orders, the kitchen (service) cooks the business logic, the storekeeper (repository) fetches ingredients (data), and DI is the manager wiring the right staff to each station - while the health inspector (tests) checks every dish before service.
keyPoints: ASP.NET minimal API: app.MapGet("/hi", () => "hello") exposes an endpoint in one line.
Dependency injection: register services in Program.cs and receive them via constructor parameters.
Records model immutable data: record Point(int X, int Y); gives value equality and with-expressions for free.
Nullable reference types (string?) catch null bugs at compile time - enable <Nullable>enable</Nullable>.
xUnit: [Fact] tests, Arrange-Act-Assert shape, Assert.Equal(expected, actual).
Separate concerns: controllers stay thin, services hold logic, repositories own data access - each testable in isolation.

practice.question: Model an immutable Money record with Amount and Currency.
Write an xUnit test asserting Reverse("abc") == "cba".
Why inject interfaces instead of new-ing a service?
practice.answer: Coding to an interface lets tests substitute a fake and lets DI swap implementations without editing consumers - the Dependency Inversion Principle in action.

interview.question: What problem does dependency injection solve?
interview.answer: It inverts control: classes receive dependencies instead of creating them. This decouples components, enables unit testing with fakes, and centralises lifetime/configuration in one composition root.

interview.question: record vs class vs struct - modern guidance?
interview.answer: record: immutable data with value equality and with-copies (DTOs, events). class: mutable reference types with identity. struct: small value types copied on assignment. Prefer records for data, classes for behaviour.

interview.question: How do you unit test an async method?
interview.answer: Make the test async Task and await the method, then assert. xUnit supports async [Fact] tests - avoid async void and .Result/.Wait() which can deadlock and hide exceptions.

interview.question: Why separate controllers, services and repositories?
interview.answer: Each layer has one responsibility and one reason to change. Controllers handle HTTP, services hold business rules, repositories own persistence - so each is independently testable and replaceable without touching the others.
